Situation in J & K
 
40.       With the installation of a newly elected Government in Jammu & Kashmir, a new ray of hope has glimmered

98th Report of Committee on Home Affairs
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Home%20Affairs/98threport.htm[30-06-2016 17:57:49]
leading to a sense of confidence among the people that peace still has a chance in their beleaguered State.  The policy of
providing ‘healing touch’ to the innumerable wounds inflicted by cross-border terrorism on the people, has been widely
welcomed as it is expected to dawn a new beginning for the people who have been subjected to one of the worst kinds of
terrorism witnessed in independent India.  In other words, a fresh process has been initiated to build bridges between the
tormented people and their elected representatives.  While following such a policy, abundant caution is called for on the
part of the Government especially to ensure that the morale of the security forces is not affected in any way. 
 
40.1     The cross-border terrorism continues unabated and efforts are on by Pakistan to further intensify this most
consistent and persistent element of its policy towards India.  The killing of innocent men, women and children in
Nadimarg Village of Pulwama district of Jammu & Kashmir is the latest case to prove that masters of the militants sitting
across the border are sparing no efforts to intensify their anti-India campaign. The brutal killings at Nadimarg reminds the
Committee of another gory incident which took place three years ago in which scores of innocent people belonging to Sikh
community were massacred at Chitisingpura Village of Anantnag district of Jammu & Kashmir.  We have come a long
distance from Chitisingpura to Nadimarg but the issue of providing foolproof security to the people including minority
communities living in the State remains unaddressed.  It is also a severe setback to the policy of reconciliation adopted by
the new Government of the State.  The Nadimarg incident has dealt a death blow, at least for the time being, to the plans to
rehabilitate the migrant Kashmiris back to their ancestral places.  Thus, once again, militants and their masters have
succeeded in engendering a great deal of terror in the minds of people of Jammu & Kashmir.  Despite the killings of the
minorities, the militants failed to arouse communal passions as majority community condemned the killings spontaneously
and provided succour to the families of the  victims.
 
 40.2    The situation, thus, calls for immediate review of the strategy to counter the violence being perpetrated by
the militants.  While fully endorsing the policy of healing touch, this Committee is of the view that the guard against
militancy should not be allowed to lower until it is completely rooted out.  As regards the security of the minorities
and other civilians, the Committee recommends with all emphasis at its command that strong multi-layer security
rings should be thrown around the areas inhabited by vulnerable sections of the people with a view to deter any
attack on them by the militants. 
Left Wing Extremism
 
41.       Left wing extremism is proving to be a serious challenge to the internal security of the country.  In 2002, a sudden
spurt has been witnessed in the level of violence by left wing extremists.  During the year, 1465 incidents of violence have
been reported as against 1208 incidents in 2001.  Today, its tentacles have spread to new areas also such as North
Chattisgarh, Western districts of West Bengal, parts of North Bihar, Eastern UP and Eastern and Southern Jharkhand.  In
all, 53 districts in 9 States of the country are under the sway of this movement.  The Government of India along with the
Governments of the affected States has been adopting a two pronged strategy which aims at neutralizing the cadres of the
extremist outfits, PWG and MCC and at the same time focusing its attention on developmental activities in the affected
areas.  A number of steps have been taken on the law & order front to control the situation.  On economic and development
front, the Ministry of Home Affairs has sent a proposal to the Planning Commission for the inclusion of these 53 affected
districts in its new scheme ‘Backward Districts Initiative’ so that additional funds are earmarked to remove their socio-
economic backwardness as per this scheme.  This apart, moves are afoot to ensure good governance and make the
administrative machinery more responsive, sensitive and transparent in the affected areas.  Effective public grievances
redressal system is also proposed to be put in place.
 
41.1     The strategy being adopted by the affected States with the assistance of the Union Government does not seem to be
yielding desired results.  Although the Government can always claim success of its strategy by furnishing figures of the
extremists killed, arrested and surrendered, the bottom line is that this problem is gradually spiralling.  The growth and
spread of the movement may be attributed to its growing clout amongst the common people.  The extremists appear to have
apparently been able to strike the right chord with the people as they have been successful in convincing a section of the
people that the State and its machinery are mainly responsible for all their woes.  This is precisely the reason for a complete
drought of intelligence inputs from the people living in affected areas.  People appear to prefer extremists over the police
and other Government agencies when it comes to making a choice between the two.  It is unfortunate that people like the
extremists, are also losing faith in the State.  Therefore, the need of the hour is to restore people’s faith in the State and its
agencies.  To the contrary, the focus of the strategy to tackle the problem appears to be more on dealing with it purely as a
law and order problem than on striking at its socio-economic roots.  As a matter of fact, no serious efforts have so far been
made to go into the socio-economic causes of the problem with a view to find a lasting solution to it.  Innocent people are
caught between the extremists and the law enforcement agencies and thus are victims at the hands of both.  On the one
hand, people are forced, at gun point, to provide food and shelter to ultras and on the other, they are subjected to harassment

98th Report of Committee on Home Affairs
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Home%20Affairs/98threport.htm[30-06-2016 17:57:49]
by the police for providing refuge to the extremists.  This leads to the alienation of the people from the State who then tend
to side with the extremists.
41.2     With these views in mind, this Committee in its 88 th Report in 2002 on Demands for Grants (2002-03) had
recommended that the Government should engage the extremist groups in a dialogue so as to arrive at a peaceful solution to
the problem.  To the Committee’s dismay, the Government has not taken its suggestion in the right perspective.  In its
ATRs on 88 th Report, the Ministry of Home Affairs stated that there was a need to seek political consensus on the issue
after consultation with Chief Ministers of the States affected by left wing extremist activities.  Accordingly, it was proposed
to discuss this issue in a meeting with the concerned Chief Ministers.  The Government of Andhra Pradesh, on an appeal
made by the Committee of Concerned  Citizens, had entered into talks with the representatives of the People’s War Group
(PWG).  The experience of Government of Andhra Pradesh will also have to be taken into account before the Central
Government considers a process of dialogue with left extremist groups operating in the country.  Further in response to a
question as to the outcome of talks between PWG and Government of Andhra Pradesh, the Ministry has replied that the
State Government of Andhra Pradesh held three rounds of talks with PWG representatives on 5 June 2002, 9 June 2002 and
20 June 2002 and it was decided to hold direct talks with PWG leaders from July 20, 2002.  However, in the meantime, on
7 July 2002, PWG emissaries withdrew as mediators in protest against police encounters.  As informed by the State
Government, the PWG tried to gain time and prolong the talks to utilize the period of respite for recruitment of cadres,
collection of information on political leaders, police officers and police stations, collection and dumping of money in safe
places, taking up land struggles and forming organizations like Telangana Jana Sabha.  The PWG is reported to have
committed 88 offences including 70 murders since the process of talks started.  On 19 July 2002, PWG withdrew itself
from talk process and declared that it will commence its actions against State and Police forces.  The Government of
Andhra Pradesh is still ready to hold talks with CPML (PW) if they lay down arms and give up violent activities.  The talks
between Andhra Pradesh State Government and PW were not successful and failed to yield any result.  The Central
Government is willing to support any peace dialogue the State Government propose to have with the LWE groups within
the framework of the Indian Constitution. 
 
41.3       In response to a question as to what precludes the Government of India in taking its own initiative to find a
peaceful solution to the problem as it is doing in the case of Naga peace talks, the Ministry has stated that ‘Public Order’
and ‘Police’ are the State subjects and it is primarily for the State Government to devise a strategy including possibility of
peace talks to counter extremism.  On its part, the Central Government is willing to support any such talks within the ambit
of the Indian Constitution. 
 
41.4     The Committee reiterates its earlier recommendation that the Government of India should come forward to initiate a
broad based peace process to put an end to the ongoing menace of left wing extremism by ensuring full involvement of
concerned States.  This being a long standing problem, the Government of India should consider playing a more proactive
role in the matter.
 
Modernisation of State Police Forces
 
42.       Police is synonymous with Government. Hence its strength and efficiency should always be upto the mark for
continuance of a Government especially a democratic one.  Keeping this in mind the Central Government took up police
modernization plan in late 1960s.  The Ministry of Home Affairs has been implementing a Non-plan Scheme for
Modernisation of State Police Forces since 1969-70 on a 50:50 cost sharing basis.  However, during the period 1969-70 to
1999-2000, a total amount of Rs.536.74 crore has been released to various State Governments on account of this scheme
which is in real terms a meager sum for such a vast project.  In view of the emerging challenges and threats to the internal
security, particularly in the form of extremism, terrorism and religious fundamentalism including left-wing extremism in
some parts of the country, the annual Central allocation under the Scheme for Modernisation of the State Police Forces was
enhanced to Rs.1000 crore from 2000-01 for 10 years.  Nevertheless, the sum allocated for 2000-01 & 2001-02 could be
utilised to the extent of 71% and 43%, respectively.
 
 42.1    The Ministry replying to a question mentioned that the Scheme provides for review of implementation after every
two years.  Accordingly, a Review Committee was constituted under a Special Secretary of Ministry of Home Affairs.  The
Committee visited a few major States and observed implementation of the Scheme.  The views of the State Governments
were also obtained regarding various aspects of the Scheme.  Most of the State Governments have expressed their inability
to contribute matching share due to financial constraints as per the underlying principle of the Scheme.  The Committee
submitted its report on implementation of the scheme.  It has inter alia recommended that the funding pattern of the
Scheme needs to be changed whereby Central Government’s share should be increased to 75% out of which 50% should be

98th Report of Committee on Home Affairs
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Home%20Affairs/98threport.htm[30-06-2016 17:57:49]
in the form of grant-in-aid and 25% as loan. 
 
42.2     The Home Secretary in his presentation before the Committee on Demands for Grants (2003-04) stated that the
Central Government had been regularly reminding the States in Chief Ministers’ Conferences and through letters to the
Chief Secretaries of States, to send perspective action plans for modernisation of their Police Forces. However, the States
have been found wanting in utilising the allotted funds.  The lack of initiative on the part of a majority of States is
apparently due to their inability to spare requisite matching funds.  This has led to a situation where the Union Government
is keen to modernise the State police forces but State Governments are not too keen to implement the scheme meant for the
purpose owing to paucity of financial resources at their disposal.  This peculiar situation emanates, to a large extent, from
the federal structure of our polity.  As per the constitutional framework, the subjects of ‘Police’ and ‘Public order’ fall
within the jurisdiction of State Governments whereas the overall responsibility for maintenance of internal security has
been vested with the Union Government under Article 355.  Accordingly, creation, maintenance and supervision of police
forces including their augmentation and modernisation are the primary responsibility of the State Governments.  Therefore,
States are duty bound to ensure that their police forces are fully equipped to meet the challenges being posed on the law and
order front.  As far as maintenance of internal security is concerned, it is the Union Government which has been enjoined
upon by the Constitution to maintain it.  Thus, the founding fathers of the Constitution tried to draw a distinct line between
the jurisdiction and responsibilities of the two Governments.   However, in practice, this line has proved to be very thin and
more often than not, it has completely blurred or vanished.  This is so because what is seen as a threat to law and order also
has a direct bearing on overall internal security and vice versa.  Thus, law and order and internal security are closely
intertwined with each other.  A change in one also gets reflected in the other.  It is precisely the reason why Ministry of
Home Affairs launched a scheme for the modernisation of State police forces as it fully realized that unless the machinery
for maintenance of law & order was strengthened, it would not be able to maintain a foolproof internal security.  Now the
question arises as to why State Governments are not paying as much attention as needed to modernize their police forces? 
Why modernisation of police is not being taken up on priority by the States even though they are fully aware of the dangers
to the general law & order situation?  Here, it may be pointed out that when it comes to the control and superintendence of
police forces, the States do not want to yield even an inch of their jurisdiction.  But at the same time when it comes to
improve and strengthen their police forces, they simply raise their hands expressing their inability to do so because of
financial constraints.  The height is that most of them are not even prepared to meet half of the expenses as per the scheme
of the Union Government.  Given the situation, the Union Government must make some earnest efforts to ensure the active
participation of State Governments in modernising their police forces.  The Union Government should not have a feeling of
helplessness in convincing the State Governments to focus their attention on this issue.  After all, Article 355 places the
responsibility of protecting the States from internal disturbances on the shoulders of the Union Government.  Therefore, the
Union Government will be well within its rights if it issues necessary instructions to the State Governments to come
forward and join it in modernising their police forces in the larger interest of maintaining internal security.  Undoubtedly,
the States have to pull up their socks and exercise financial prudence so as to spare requisite funds for implementation of
the scheme.
 
42.3     The Committee while realising the importance of the role of the State Governments in modernising their police
forces is also conscious of the poor financial position of the States.  Keeping that in view it endorses the proposal which
envisages a new funding pattern based on 75:25 ratio.  This new pattern will reduce the liability of the States from present
50% to 25% of the funds to be used for the modernisation of State police forces.  Here a genuine concern arises as to what
if State Governments fail to provide even half of what they are required to provide at present.  It once again takes the
Committee back to its conclusion mentioned in the preceding paragraphs that States will have to find ways and means to
provide their share of the requisite funds.  The State Governments just cannot afford to look up to the Union Government. 
In a nutshell, the Committee while recommending a switchover to the new funding pattern of 75:25 for implementation of
the scheme, is also of the view that the Union Government should evolve a suitable mechanism to seek active participation
of State Governments in its efforts to modernise their police forces.
 
42.4     The Government of India may also consider the possibility of earmarking the States’ share for modernisation of
police forces while providing annual central plan assistance to them so as to ensure the effective participation of the States
in the implementation of the scheme for modernisation of State police forces.  The Government may further consider to
stop the release of funds so earmarked in central plan assistance in respect of States who are found wanting vis-à-vis the
implementation of the scheme for modernisation of State police forces.
 
42.5     Another issue related to the scheme for modernisation of State police forces is the monitoring of the implementation
of this scheme and the assessment of the actual benefits of the scheme accrued to the States. There has always been an
element of doubt over the actual benefits that accrue to the States out of a centrally sponsored scheme because the actual

98th Report of Committee on Home Affairs
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Home%20Affairs/98threport.htm[30-06-2016 17:57:49]
implementation of the scheme rests with the concerned State Governments. Although there is a provision for review of the
implementation of the scheme by Ministry of Home Affairs after every two years, there is no credible information available
to assess the actual benefits. All that is available is the details of the funds allocated to various States over the years.
Moreover, the periodic review done in two years’ time is more of a routine bureaucratic exercise. Therefore, the need of the
hour is that a specialised central agency should be entrusted with the task to oversee the implementation of this scheme. It is
the Committee’s considered view that there can be no better agency than BPR&D to be entrusted with this task. BPR&D
has the expertise and experience to take upon itself this responsibility. All that it requires is necessary manpower and
wherewithal to perform this duty. By entrusting this task to the BPR&D, a constant, regular and effective monitoring of the
scheme can be ensured which will bring about a sea change in the way this scheme is being implemented and monitored at
present.  The Committee is also of the view that it should be made mandatory for BPR&D to submit quarterly status reports
in respect of the beneficiary States vis-à-vis the implementation of this scheme.
 
42.6     Another aspect of the scheme for modernisation of State police forces which needs a re-look is the question as to
whether the present scheme of allotting funds to the State Governments should continue or it should be replaced by a
scheme whereby the central assistance is given in kind and not in cash as it is being done in the case of North-Eastern
States.  Here it may again be worth mentioning that the real benefits of centrally sponsosred schemes fail to reach the
intended beneficiaries quite often than not as a result of which the purpose behind a scheme gets defeated.  Keeping this
view in mind, it is felt that whatever assistance is to be extended to the States it should be in kind and not in cash.  There are
a couple of benefits of following this policy.  One, uniformity in providing standard equipments/gadgets can be ensured to
all the States.  Second, the apprehensions regarding misutilisation of allotted funds can be removed.  Third, the speedy
implementation of a scheme can be ensured if equipment/gadgets are procured at the central level and made available to the
States directly thereby doing away with the usual cumbersome cycle starting from allocation of funds to the final
procurement and installation of equipment/gadgets.
 
42.7     In case of the scheme for modernisation of State police forces, there are two aspects.  One, it aims at improving the
physical infrastructure such as police stations, police posts, buildings, etc.  And the other is the provision of modern
weaponry, equipment, gadgetry, computers, etc. to the police forces to improve their strike capability and general
functioning.  As far as the first aspect is concerned, the present scheme involving release of funds needs no change for
obvious reasons.  It is the second aspect, which happens to be crucial from the point of view of improving the strike
capability of the police forces, that needs a shift from cash to kind.  The Committee is of the view that under the scheme for
modernisation of police forces, only a part of the central share of the funds should be allotted to the States in cash to meet
their requirements  for improving physical infrastructure such as police stations, etc.  Insofar as weaponry, gadgetry,
equipment, vehicles, etc., the central assistance should always be in kind for the reasons stated in the preceding paragraphs.
 
Delhi Police
 
43.       Policing a city like Delhi is in itself a stupendous task.  Delhi Police has been engaged in this task for long.
However with the passage of every single day its task is becoming more difficult and complex as the population of the city
is growing constantly.  To cope up with the situation, Delhi Police needs updating its strength, technology and
infrastructure.   Keeping in view the need for modernisation as well as the need to enable Delhi Police to meet the emerging
challenges, BPR&D was entrusted with the task of studying manpower requirements and modernisational needs of Delhi
Police. BPR&D in its Report has touched almost every aspect of police functioning.  It has been more than two years since
BPR&D submitted its Study Report.  Unfortunately, its recommendations have not yet been implemented.  The Report is
still moving back and forth between North Block and Indraprastha Estate.  In this entire process, the Study Report, which
has since been accepted in principle by the Ministry of Home Affairs, has become victim of procrastination and
bureaucratic apathy.  Had this not been true, the Ministry would have come up with a definite timeframe and cost estimates
to implement the Report.  Instead, the Ministry is still groping in the dark.  There is clear ambivalence and lack of
enthusiasm in the Ministry of Home Affairs vis-à-vis the implementation of this Report.  In sharp contrast to this, the same
Ministry prepares, with the help of CPMFs, a perspective plan having a definite timeframe and concrete budgetary
proposals for the modernisation and augmentation of CPMFs, seeks the approval of the Cabinet for the plan and sets the
plan in motion.  Not just that, the Ministry is now in the process of finalising a modernisation plan for SSB also, which has
acquired the status of a CPMF of late.  But when it comes to Delhi Police, why there is so much ambivalence in the
approach of the Ministry of Home Affairs?  Instead of taking the onus upon itself for the implementation of the Report, it
either passes the buck on to the BPR&D for not quantifying the expenditure for implementing its recommendations or
drops the ball in the court of Delhi Police by asking it to prioritise its requirements.  Here the question arises as to whether
the quantification of the expenditure to be incurred in implementing its recommendations was included in the terms of
reference given to the BPR&D?  If not, how can the Ministry wash its hands off by saying that BPR&D did not quantify the

43.1.1  It is good that the Delhi Police has submitted concrete proposals after working out the costs involved in their
implementation.  It, however, has not indicated any timeframe for their implementation.  Now it is for the Ministry of
Home Affairs to see that proposals are implemented in a time bound manner so as to begin with the implementation of the
recommendations of BPR&D.  This limited implementation of the recommendations of BPR&D, however, does not
condone the piecemeal manner in which the Ministry intends to implement them.  What is more important and of primary
focus for this Committee is the implementation of BPR&D’s Study Report in its totality within a stipulated timeframe and
with necessary budgetary allocations.
 
43.1.2  Therefore, the Committee while reiterating its earlier recommendations in its 73
rd and 88th Reports on Demands for
Grants (2001-02) and (2002-03), respectively, once again exhorts upon the Ministry of Home Affairs to draw a clear cut
time schedule and quantify the expenditure to be incurred for implementing the recommendations of BPR&D contained in
its Study Report on manpower requirements and modernisational needs of Delhi Police.  The Committee is of the opinion
that the Ministry of Home Affairs, after having drawn a definite time schedule and worked out the costs to be involved in
implementing the recommendations, should seek the approval of the Cabinet for necessary budgetary allocations for that
purpose.      
 
43.2     For a city like Delhi which has the distinction of having the largest number of motor vehicles compared to any other
city in the country, management of ever-growing road traffic should receive utmost attention of the Government with a
long-term perspective.  To the contrary, the Government is more keen to focus on short-term measures rather than finding
some long-term solutions to the numerous problems doting Delhi’s traffic scenario.  This Committee, with a view to look
for a proper mechanism for evolving a long-term perspective plan for management of traffic in Delhi, had recommended for
setting up a Unified Traffic Management Authority in its 73
rd Report on Demands for Grants (2001-02) and reiterated it in
its 88th Report on Demands for Grants (2002-03).  On both the occasions, the Ministry of Home Affairs had replied that the
recommendation of the Committee was forwarded to the Government of Delhi which, in turn, has stated that under the
existing constitutional scheme of governance for the National Capital Territory, it may not be possible to bring about an
integrated legislation to set up a Unified Traffic Management Authority.  The matter is, however, being examined by the
Government.  Here, the notable fact is that in its two consecutive ATRs, the Ministry has maintained the same position.  In
last three years, it has not been able to wriggle out of the constitutional quandary as to which of the two Governments is
competent to set up this authority.  Is three years’ time too little to solve this so-called puzzle ?  Given the existing scheme
of constitutional relationship between the Government of Delhi and Government of India, the onus of setting up this
authority is on the Ministry of Home Affairs, as Delhi has still not attained full-fledged statehood.  Besides, matters
pertaining to ‘Police’ and ‘Land’ in relation to NCT of Delhi fall within the jurisdiction of Union Government.  Therefore,
the Committee is of the considered view that Ministry of Home affairs should take immediate steps to set up a Unified
Traffic Management Authority for Delhi.
 
43.3     Housing needs of the personnel of Delhi Police is another important area which has been a cause of concern for this
Committee. It has been expressing its deep concern on this issue for the last four years in its 54

43.3.1  Keeping this in view, the Committee fully endorses the view that Delhi Police should be allowed to acquire more
and more ready-built-flats in order to raise the satisfaction level in respect of the residential accommodation for its
personnel.  This should be the policy decision to meet not only the present but also the future housing requirements of Delhi
Police.  The success of this measure will, however, hinge on the allocation of requisite funds.  Accordingly, the Committee
strongly feels that the Government should not only allocate Rs.79 crore to enable Delhi Police to purchase 520 odd flats in
Dwarka sub-city of Delhi for the present but it should also make necessary budgetary provisions for further purchase of
flats by Delhi Police.
 
43.4     Traffic scenario of Delhi continues to be as chaotic as it can get with one problem after the other rearing its head. 
The problems are such which cannot and will not submit to solutions which are one time and adhoc in nature.  Consistence
and persistence should be the guiding principles for any enforcement policy.  The adherence to this principle is more
appropriate than elsewhere in a city like Delhi whose roads witness one of the worst kinds of lawlessness.  One such
problem is the use of high decibel pressure horns used mainly by private passenger buses and other commercial vehicles
plying in the city.  Although, Delhi Police takes punitive action against the vehicles fitted with pressure horns, the situation
is far from being under control.  Here, a special mention may be made of the private passenger buses plying under Stage
Carriage Scheme of State Transport Authority which are invariably fitted with pressure horns.  The drivers of these buses
blare pressure horns with impunity and thus cause immense noise pollution which continues unabated.  Interestingly, Delhi
Traffic Police is finding it beyond its means to check the use of pressure horns by a few thousands of buses plying in Delhi. 
Apparently, there is lack of persistence in the enforcement drive to rid the city of these ear deafening horns.  All that is
needed to be done is not being done.  The way the operators of these buses are being allowed to get away with, after
causing immense damage to the health of the people, it appears that some kind of complicity exists between them and
certain levels of Delhi Traffic Police. 
 
43.4.1  Therefore, the Committee is of the view that the situation warrants immediate action on the part of Delhi Traffic
Police to see that Delhites get rid of this menace of pressure horns once and for all.  The Committee recommends that the
Delhi Traffic Police should not only immediately launch a citywide drive against the use of pressure horns especially by
private passenger buses but should also sustain it till such time the city is declared “Free of Pressure Horns”.  It is also of
the view that stringent measures should be taken to prohibit not just the use of pressure horns but also their sale, purchase
and possession within the municipal limits of Delhi.  The Committee would like to take stock of the situation after the lapse
of three months from the date of presentation of its Report in the wake of its above stated recommendation. 
 
Modernisation of Central Para Military Forces (CPMFs)
 
44.       The Central Para Military Forces (CPMFs) have been playing a very crucial role in thwarting both external and
internal threats to the security of the nation.  The vital role being played by them can very well be understood by the fact
that most of these forces are deployed to nearly 100% of their strength which also means that their reserves too are fully
deployed.  This shows how strenuous and difficult is the nature of the duties being performed by the personnel of CPMFs. 
While performing various tasks assigned to them, these forces not only have had to maintain a constant pressure on their

98th Report of Committee on Home Affairs
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Home%20Affairs/98threport.htm[30-06-2016 17:57:49]
adversaries such as militants, insurgents, mercenaries, etc. by way of dynamic deployment, they also have to bear in mind
that their weaponry, gadgetry, equipment, etc. are in no way inferior to those of their adversaries.  With a view to enhance
their striking capabilities in terms of better firepower and a fully equipped manpower, the modernisation plans of six
CPMFs, namely, BSF, CRPF, NSG, CISF, ITBP and Assam Rifles have been put underway.  The modernisation plan for
the seventh CPMF i.e. SSB is also under consideration of the Ministry of Home Affairs.  The notable feature of this
modernisation exercise is that it is being carried out as per a comprehensive perspective plan with concrete budgetary
allocations spread over a time frame of five years.  These modernisation plans inter alia aim at augmentation of the
manpower of the CPMFs.  Accordingly, in all 209 battalions have been sanctioned for CPMFs including India Reserve (IR)
Battalions and Rashtriya Rifles.  Out of these 209 battalions, 127 battalions have been sanctioned to be raised during 2000-
01, 2001-02 and 2002-03.  The remaining 82 battalions are proposed to be raised during 2003-04 and 2004-05 at the rate of
41 battalions in each year.  While the battalions/companies sanctioned during   2000-01 and 2001-02 have already been
raised, the battalions sanctioned for 2002-03 are in the process of raising.
 
44.1     This Committee has all along been in favour of strengthening the CPMFs and will continue to support any
measure/proposal aimed at keeping them in tune with changing times in future too.  While the Committee fully endorses the
on-going exercise of modernisation and augmentation of CPMFs, it, however, would tend to draw the attention of the
Ministry of Home Affairs to some of the practical difficulties being faced by the forces in the wake of the implementation
of their modernisation plans.  The Committee is given to understand that most of the newly sanctioned battalions being
raised are, in effect, nothing but addition of a few more companies to the existing battalions.  The net result of this exercise
is that instead of raising new battalions which have their own infrastructure, chain of command, area of operation, etc., the
existing battalions are being stuffed with more personnel without any support paraphernalia.  For instance, 38 companies
have been sanctioned to ITBP to convert its 19 battalions from 4 company pattern to 6 company pattern.  But administration
staff such as cooks, washerman, barber and water carrier, and support staff for telecom, motor transport, animal transport,
dog squad, etc. have not been sanctioned.  The lack of administration and support staff not only renders the additional
companies operationally dysfunctional but also puts extra strain on the already stretched out infrastructure of the existing
battalions.  Therefore, in view of the situation as explained above, the Committee expresses the view that necessary
paraphernalia should be provided to the additional companies being raised as per the modernisation plans of CPMFs.  It is
of the opinion that the very purpose behind modernisation and augmentation plans will be defeated if the additional
battalions/companies are rendered dysfunctional due to lack of necessary support system.
 
44.2     As mentioned elsewhere in this Report, the process of raising 127 battalions out of the total 209 newly sanctioned
battalions of CPMFs including IR battalions and Rashtriya Rifles, is due for completion by the close of the financial year
2002-03.  With the raising of these 127 battalions, it is expected that CPMFs will be able to relieve their reserve battalions
from various areas of operation.  Accordingly, the Committee recommends that as soon as these127 battalions are fully
operationalised, the reserve battalions of all CPMFs should be withdrawn from operational duties to the extent possible. 
With the withdrawal of reserve battalions, the Committee hopes that sufficient number of jawans could be spared for
training, etc. so as not only to improve the quality of manpower but also to reduce the stress level of the jawans.
 
44.3     Another closely related aspect of the modernisation and augmentation process of CPMFs is the quality of their
human resource.  While there is no gainsaying the fact that CPMFs need to be modernised and their strength needs
augmentation but at the same time we should not lose sight of the quality of their manpower.  In our attempt to see that our
security forces are not outnumbered by their adversaries, we should not end up raising a huge army of jawans who are not
properly looked after, are not provided with quality diet, clothes, accessories, etc. and are not spared for sufficient relief and
recreation.  In addition, welfare measures are also not compromised.  In the view of the Committee, there is an urgent need
to focus on the well being of the jawans of CPMFs so as to improve their allround development.  Accordingly, it
recommends that the Government should lay equal emphasis on the quality of manpower of CPMFs while making attempts
to augment their quantity.
 
44.4     The living conditions for jawans in the barracks of CPMFs also need mention.  The Committee is given to
understand that the upkeep of the barracks is very poor which has a direct impact on the health and well being of jawans. 
Lack of proper attention, adequate funds, etc. are some of the reasons behind the poor conditions in the barracks.  The
Committee, therefore, recommends that adequate funds should be earmarked to improve living conditions in the barracks of
the jawans.  Besides, strict and clear guidelines should be issued to ensure proper upkeep of the barracks.

45.       No other issue than the housing requirements of the personnel of Central Para Military Forces has attracted the

grossly inefficient totally unequipped to complete the housing projects of CPMFs?
 
45.1     Given the state of affairs as they are in respect of the execution of housing projects of CPMFs by CPWD, the
Committee is constrained to observe that Ministry of Urban Development is adopting inflexible attitude by not allowing a
general relaxation under GFR 136 for the housing projects of CPMFs.  It is this attitude of Ministry of Urban Development
which is now proving to be an even bigger hurdle than the GFR 136 itself.  Keeping this in view, the Committee is of the
considered view that the Ministry of Home Affairs should approach the Cabinet to seek a general exemption under GFR
136 for the housing projects of CPMFs located anywhere in the country so as to enable the CPMFs to get their housing
projects executed through public sector construction companies.
 
Border Security Force (BSF)
 
46.       Border Security Force (BSF) is one of India’s premier border guarding forces which is not only performing its
primary role of guarding borders but also playing an equally important role in the maintenance of internal security in
Jammu & Kashmir. At present it has 157 battalions which are fully deployed. The role of BSF in guarding Line of Control
(LoC) as well as maintenance of internal security in Jammu & Kashmir needs special mention. Out of 778 Km. long LoC,
BSF has been entrusted with guarding a long stretch of 237.20 Km. while rest of the LoC is under the direct command of
army. Similarly, its 49 battalions have been entrusted with counter insurgency duties in Jammu & Kashmir where also it is
playing an equally important role as that of army. The Director-General, BSF, in his presentation before the Committee
stated that as a matter of fact BSF is standing shoulder to shoulder with the army whether it is counter-insurgency duties or
maintaining a vigil on and guarding as crucial an area as LoC. The nature of duties being performed by BSF personnel is
same as that of the army personnel. But when it comes to payment of allowances, there is a wide gap between the
allowances admissible to the personnel of two forces. The allowances being paid to the army personnel are much higher
than the ones being paid to the BSF personnel for performing the duties which are not only equal in nature and intensity but
also involve equal physical endurance with extremely high stress and fatigue levels.
 
46.1     In view of the above, the Committee recommends that the Government should look into the anomalies.

47.       Special Service Bureau was set up in early 1963 in the wake of Indo-China conflict of 1962 to build people’s morale

and inculcate a spirit of resistance in border population in the then NEFA, North Assam, North Bengal, hills of Uttar
Pradesh and Jammu & Kashmir (Ladakh).  Later SSB’s area of operation was extended to other border areas in Manipur,
Tripura, Jammu, Meghalaya, Sikkim, Rajasthan, Gujarat, Mizoram, South Bengal and Nagaland.
 
47.1     The main role of the organisation was to promote national integration and security consciousness amongst border
population, win over the hearts and minds of the people through participative developmental programmes in remote
inaccessible border areas, help rescue and relief operations during natural calamities, counter enemy propaganda through
multi-dimensional publicity campaigns and bring the population in the national mainstream.  The organization undertook a
variety of confidence building and perception management activities and came to be perceived as a friend and ambassador
of goodwill by the local people.  However, the role and charter of SSB stand thoroughly revised pursuant to the acceptance
of the recommendations of Group of Ministers (GoM) on reforming the national security system.  SSB has now been
entrusted with the task of guarding the Indo-Nepal border with effect from January 2001.  Accordingly, the present role and
charter of SSB in its new incarnation as a Central Para Military Force (CPMF) is to guard Indo-Nepal border, to promote a
sense of security amongst the people living in the border areas, to prevent trans-border crimes and unauthorised entry into
or exit from the territory of India and to prevent smuggling and any other illegal activities.
 
47.2     With the change in its role and charter, SSB, which was initially conceptualized as an intelligence gathering and
confidence building agency in the border areas, is now an exclusively combative force.  This transformation of SSB into a
CPMF has put a big question mark on the fate and career growth of its civilian staff who were hitherto performing the
duties as per its original role and charter.  Since the new objective of the force is primarily to guard Indo-Nepal border, the
focus will now be entirely shifted to the combatised component of its personnel.  This can be substantiated with the help of
a decision taken by Ministry of Home Affairs that from now on there will be no more recruitment in the civilian cadres.  It
has also been decided that vacancies in civilian cadres will be filled by combatised personnel.  Evidently, the non-
combatised wing or civilian wing of SSB has now been completely orphaned.  As per the new scheme of things, the civilian
wing will be allowed to die its natural death.
 
47.3     In view of the above, the Committee recommends that the Government should look into the problems of civilian
cadre of SSB.
 
Modernisation of Prisons
 
48.       Prisons as a subject comes under State List of the seventh schedule to the constitution and as such it is the primary
responsibility of the State Governments to look after every aspect of prison administration such as construction,
maintenance, expansion, renovation, etc. of jails.  Unfortunately, the conditions in jails across the country are really pathetic
partly due to negligence and partly due to indifference of the authorities to maintain healthy and hygienic conditions.  Lack
of funds is another reasons for poor state of affairs in the prisons.  As a result of all this, the prisons all across the country
are overcrowded with poor living conditions for the inmates.  With a view to reduce overcrowding in jails and improve
general conditions prevailing in them, the Ministry of Home Affairs has been implementing a scheme for modernization of
prisons.  From the financial year 2002-03, the Ministry has started implementing a five year perspective plan for
modernization of prisons having an outlay of Rs.1800 crore.  The scheme has been prepared by the Ministry with the
assistance of BPR&D.  The scheme is to be implemented with the cost sharing ratio of 75:25 between the Centre and States
respectively.  Rs.270 crore will be provided by the Central Government and Rs.90 crore by the State Governments every
year during the next five years.  The scheme focuses on the following areas:
(a)
                Construction of additional jails to reduce overcrowding at the cost of Rs.1034.60 crore;
(b)               Repair and renovation of existing jails at the cost of Rs.248.65 crore;
(c)                Improvement in sanitation and water supply at the cost of Rs.48.25 crore; and
(d)               Living accommodation for prisons staff at the cost of Rs.465.05 crore.
 
48.1     The Committee is happy to note that the Ministry of Home Affairs is taking initiatives to modernise the prisons. 
But as in the case of the implementation of the scheme for modernisation of State police forces, in case of this scheme too,
the Committee apprehends that real benefits of the scheme may not accrue due to improper implementation by the State
Governments and not so effective monitoring by the Ministry of Home Affairs.  The Committee, therefore, recommends
that the implementation of this scheme should be effectively implemented.
 
48.2     The Committee is also of the view that the existing prisons wherever located on prime lands should be relocated and
the money received from the sales of their prime lands may be utilised for building spacious and modern prisons.

Criminal Justice System
 
49.       Crime has been defined as an offence against the society or   community.  The primary object of criminal law is to
preserve and maintain public order.  Besides, a firm but humane application of criminal law is essential for the proper
functioning of constitutional democracy.  Otherwise, the consequence would be one of lawlessness and anarchy.  Herein,
lies the importance of criminal law and its role in establishing a sound criminal justice administration.
49.1     However, Criminal Justice System in India has been suffering from hangover of British rule as well as some
inherent lacunae.  The reason being the inadvertence of the Government to reform the laws to suit the time.  The long
period of trial and the undertrials being in prisons for longer periods than the maximum of punishment provided for the
offence have been a major cause of concern.  In addition to these, the problem of hostile witnesses is hampering the
prosecutions.  A police officer records statements during the course of investigation and submits them with other relevant
evidence to the court along with the chargesheet.  One can well understand how weakened the prosecution case will
become if key persons such as eye-witnesses or the complainant himself/herself changes the original version to the police
while deposing in court.
 
49.2     The Home Secretary in his presentation before the Committee mentioned that the Government has already set up a
Committee under the Chairmanship of Dr. (Justice) V.S. Malimath, retired Chief Justice of Kerala High Court to
recommend the measures for revamping the Criminal Justice System.  The Home Secretary also informed that the
Malimath Committee is expected to submit its report by 31 March 2003.  He also mentioned that on the recommendations
of Malimath Committee a time bound programme would be drawn out for its implementation.
 
49.3     In the backdrop of all these developments the Committee recommends that the reform in the Criminal Justice
System should be expedited as it finds that the Malimath Committee has kept on taking extensions whereas the subject
demands immediate attention and action.  The Committee strongly feels that the process of investigation, prosecution and
adjudication should be simplified, thus making cheap, expeditious and swift justice available to the people.  This will have
a positive effect on the prison administration as well, which are crowded with undertrial prisoners.  
 
Border Management
 
50.       India shares long international borders with its neighbours.  A considerable stretch of its borders pass through very
rough and undulating terrain which makes the task of border guarding an extremely difficult one.  This apart, inclement
weather conditions ranging from sub-zero temperatures to more than 50 degree celsius temperatures test the endurance and
commitment of the forces deployed to maintain vigil along the borders.  These hostile natural and weather conditions while
on the one hand make it very difficult for the forces to check cross-border movement of people, on the other hand these
very conditions prove advantageous for militants, immigrants, extremists, mercenaries and smugglers, etc. as they manage
to sneak in and out of the country because of the porosity of borders.  The need for reducing porosity of borders as also to
plug the holes in the borders being used by militants, insurgents etc. as gateways for infiltration into and exfiltration out of
India, has since long been felt.  However, it was in the wake of Kargil intrusions that attention was paid to the management
of borders in a more systematic manner.  The Group of Ministers (GoM) on reforming national security system inter alia
recommended for creating a separate Department of Border Management in the Ministry of Home Affairs.  The
Government has since accepted the recommendation and to begin with has set up a Border Management Division which
will later be transformed into a full-fledged Department.  Thus, Border Management has assumed greater significance
keeping in view the fact that maintenance of internal security depends to a large extent on how we manage our borders. 
The Government has now adopted ‘one border-one force’ principle with a view to have one dedicated border guarding
force for one border.
 
50.1     The Committee is happy to note that the Government is now paying focused attention to manage country’s long
borders with its neighbours.  Border guarding is the primary duty of the Central forces deployed on various borders.  Apart
from having coordination and cooperation among border guarding forces, various intelligence agencies and State police, the
country should have a border management policy with a long-term perspective to deal not just with present but also with
future threats.  Therefore, the Committee is of the view that the Government should take necessary steps to ensure effective
coordination and cooperation among border guarding forces, army, various intelligence agencies and State police.  At the
same time, it should frame a broad policy for border management with a long-term perspective to meet present as well as
future challenges on our frontiers.

51.0     The Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) is the premier investigating police agency in the country. It traces its
origin to the Special Police Establishment (SPE) which was set up way back in 1941 by the then Government of India to
investigate cases of bribery and corruption in the War & Supply Department of India during World War II.  The Delhi
Special Police Establishment (DSPE) Act, 1946 inter alia makes provision of constitution, powers, functions of SPE and
offences to be investigated by it.  Subsequently, the purview of SPE was enlarged to cover all Departments of the
Government of India and the jurisdiction was extended to all the Union Territories and could also be extended to the States
with the consent of the State Governments concerned.
 
51.1     The CBI  was created through a resolution of Ministry of Home Affairs dated April 1, 1963 to administer DPSE
Act, 1946, following which the DPSE is popularly known as the  CBI.  As per  Section 3 of DPSE Act, 1946, CBI/DPSE
could investigate those offences/classes of offences  notified in Official Gazette by the Government of India. Initially, the
offences that were notified by the Central Government related only to corruption by Central Government employees.  In
due course, with the setting up of a large number of Public Sector Undertakings, the employees of those undertakings were
also brought under the purview of  CBI.  Similarly, with the nationalization of the Banks in 1969, the Public Sector Banks
and their employees also came within the ambit of the CBI.  By now, the CBI  has become multi-disciplinary  investigative
agency with its expanding role from corruption cases to other cases viz – cyber crime, terrorist crime, wildlife crime,
narcotics, arms trafficking, arts and antiquities cases, counterfeiting of currencies, etc.
 
51.2     The SPE initially had two Wings, namely, (i)  the General Offences Wing (GOW) and (ii) Economic Offences Wing
(EOW).  The GOW dealt with cases of bribery and corruption involving the employees of Central Government and Public
Sector Undertakings.  The EOW dealt with cases of violation of various economic/fiscal laws.  Apart from this, the CBI
investigates cases referred to it by the Supreme Court ,various High Courts and the State Governments.
 
51.2.1  The CBI was divided into two investigative Divisions, namely, (i) Anti Corruption Division (ACD) and (ii) Special
Crimes Division (SCD), the latter dealing with cases of conventional crimes, besides economic offences. Again, in 1994 the
organizational structure of CBI was made into following Divisions: (i) Anti Corruption Division (ACD) (ii) Special Crime
Division (SCD) (iii) Economic Offence Division (EOD).
 
51.2.2  Three Divisions namely, Anti Corruption Division, Special Crime Division and Economic Offence Division are
Investigating Divisions.  Anti Corruption Division investigates cases of corruptions and frauds committed by public
servants of all Central Government Departments, Central Public Sector Undertakings and Financial Institutions.  Economic
Offence Division investigates economic crimes including bank frauds, cheating, financial frauds, Import Export and
Foreign Exchange violations, large scale smuggling of narcotics, antiques and other contraband items.  Special Crime
Division investigates into cases of terrorism, bomb blast, sensational homicides, kidnapping, murder and crimes committed
by the mafia/underworld. 
 
51.2.3  Following the Supreme Court Judgment of 18 December 1997, in the Vineet Narain   case, the Directorate of  
Prosecutions was set up in CBI in September 2001. The Directorate of      Prosecution is responsible for conducting
prosecution of CBI cases in various courts and also giving legal advice to CBI officers.
 
51.2.4  The CBI, through its Policy and Coordination Division coordinates investigation for the members of INTERPOLf
51.2.5  The CBI has also set up a Cyber Crime Investigation and Research Cell, which besides doing research in this field
also caters to the long felt need of the investigating agencies. It has also set up Criminal Intelligence Cell.  The
organizational structure of the CBI as on today is given below:-

from investigation has shown a satisfactorily steady pace as compared to registration. Given below in tabular form is the
number of cases registered and disposed from investigation in the last three years as furnished to the Committee:
                                                                 TABLE - III
                            Registration of Cases for Investigation vis-à-vis Disposal
    
51.7.1  With regard to disposal of trial cases, the  Director, CBI apprised the Committee that the organisation has achieved
71%, 70% and 69% in 2000, 2001 and 2002, respectively which are higher than the disposal rate of any investigating
agency in the country. In the years 1999, 2000, 2001 & 2002, cases referred to CBI for investigation are 157, 113, 155 and
142, respectively.
 
51.7.2  The Committee notes the rate of disposal  of cases for investigation  against the rate of registration.  It, therefore,
urges the Government to take every possible step so as to keep up pace with   the rate of registration of cases.
 
51.7.3  One of the important job of the Directorate of Prosecution is preparation of panel of Counsel to conduct
prosecution.  But sometimes the regular Counsel engaged by the CBI may not be able to sustain his arguments especially
before an eminent lawyer hired by the opposite party in the Court of Law resulting in low conviction rate.
 
51.7.4  The Committee therefore desires that as and when circumstances warrant the Government can engage
leading lawyers/advocates as Counsel to argue for CBI in the Court of Law to achieve high conviction rate.
 
51.7.5  The Committee also wanted to know whether a review of pending cases has been made to which  it was informed
that the CBI constantly reviews the status of pending cases on a monthly and quarterly basis, through monthly reports
obtained from all the Branches, and quarterly meetings held with the Regional Deputy Inspectors General.  In the year
2002, four such meetings were held to lay greater stress on quicker decision making.  Two meetings with the
Superintendents of Police were also held in August 2002 and February 2003.  The following steps have been taken to
reduce delays in investigation:
(i)
                  It has been decided on 10.1.2003 that in cases where only Regular Departmental Action is contemplated,
Departments/Ministries will appoint their own Presenting Officers instead of the Investigation Officer of
CBI acting as the Presenting Officer.  Thus, the Investigation Officers would have more time for
investigation purposes;
(ii)
                To expedite issue of Letters Rogatory , it has been decided that CBI will approach the Ministry of Home
Affairs direct rather than through the Administrative Department; and
(iii)               The Government is monitoring cases relating to sanction for prosecution and it is proposed to introduce a
Web- Monitoring System for effective and close monitoring.
51.7.6  The Committee feels that by appointing an officer of the Ministry as Presenting Officer in cases of departmental
enquiry, the impartiality of the investigation may be compromised.  Further, the Committee is of the considered view that
since the Presenting Officer is not an Investigating Officer, investigation by the Departmental Officer may weaken the said
process.  Therefore, the Committee recommends that a CBI officer should be the Presenting Officer in such enquiries.
 
51.7.7  With regard to cases awaiting grant of sanction for prosecution by Ministries/Departments, the Committee was
informed that a review was undertaken by the Cabinet Secretariat in a meeting held on 20.2.2003 wherein it was decided
that to make monitoring effective:
(i)
                  Cases will be segregated into less than three months and more than three months category for each
Ministry/Department;

(ii)                Segregate cases under the P.C. Act and Cr.P.C. and show them separately;
(iii)               The CVO of Department/Ministry would act as the nodal officer to closely pursue the sanctions;
(iv)              The monitoring mechanism in the Ministry/Department in respect of Public Sector undertakings would be
strengthened.
(v)                For enabling critical real-time follow up of cases pending beyond 60 days, utilisation of the web-based
software developed by the NIC would be made;
(vi)              CVC and Ministry of Law would be requested to issue appropriate internal instruction for expeditious
clearance of files referred to them for tendering advice by Ministries/Departments;
(vii)             Periodic joint meetings between the CBI, Ministries/Departments and the CVC would be revived. 
 
51.7.8  While noting the steps devised to reduce delays in investigation and monitoring the rate of disposal of cases from
investigation of CBI effective, the Committee, however, feels that the rate of conviction from trial (71% in 2000, 70% in
2001 and 69% in 2002) needs improvement.  Considering the expanding role of CBI in cyber crime, terrorist crime,
counterfeiting of currencies, arms trafficking, etc. it is obvious that unless CBI disposes cases from both investigation and
trial at the same rate of registration, pendency in both aspects is bound to be on the increase.  It, therefore, recommends that
CBI should closely and seriously monitors cases with it and increase the disposal level of cases.
 
51.7.9  The Committee observes that a number of trivial cases are being referred to the CBI.  The Committee is of the
opinion that insignificant cases should not be referred to the CBI which fritter away its energy.  The Committee
recommends to the Union Government to apply its mind in the matter and if necessary it may amend the relevant Section(s)
of the DPSE Act, 1946 so that routine cases referred to CBI for investigation, are not accepted.
 
51.7.10 The Committee has also been informed that as on 31.12.2002, 183 cases were pending sanctioned for prosecution
out of which 21 has been referred to Central Vigilance Commission (CVC) and 6 are being referred to it for its advice (See
Annexure -B for detail).
 
51.7.11 It may be pertinent to mention here that all cases pertaining to Senior Government functionaries are being sent to
CVC by the concerned Ministries/Departments to tender advice as to whether the case should be charge-sheeted, regular
departmental enquiry conducted or dropped.  Therefore, the urgency with which the CVC decides on the cases referred to it
plays a vital role in disposing the cases pending sanction for prosecution with CBI. 
 
51.7.12 The CVC should therefore be requested to assist the CBI in deciding the cases referred to it expeditiously so that
CBI could take appropriate action thereon.
 
51.8     Keeping in view the high pendency of cases under trial, the Committee wanted to know how many Special Courts,
exclusively for CBI cases, were functioning as on date along with the pendency and disposal of cases in each of these
Special Courts.  In response, the CBI furnished the following information which is produced in the accompanying Table:

Government for constitution of new courts, it had proposed for setting up of 12 new Special Courts and 6 Special
Magistrate Courts in 8 States and 1 UT to which the Central Government has accorded funding. 
 
51.9.1  Since 1997, the State Governments have been enabled to seek reimbursement of expenditure from the Central
Government for running the Special Courts set up exclusively for cases of CBI.  The expenditure towards reimbursement is
charged to the Head of Account "2055"-01.00.28-"Professional Services".  The Committee has been informed that keeping
in view the two-fold problem of (i) limited budgetary availability and (2) non-segregation  of reimbursement proposals
from other expenditure  to be charged to the head for defraying expenses incurred on Retainer Counsels, Special Counsels
etc., two requests were made by the CBI to the Department of Expenditure to-
(i)         Substantially increase the outlay in the head of account; and
(ii)        Create a minor head of account for the reimbursement to State Governments for Special Courts.
 
51.9.2  Accordingly, in the year 2002-2003 enhancement of budgetary outlay from Rs 3.8 crore in the BE to Rs.6.24 crore
has been  proposed in the RE and supplementary grants sought.  The request for creating a new minor head of account is
also under consideration of Ministry of Finance.
 
51.9.3  Taking into consideration the limitations of expanding the non-plan outlay under the minor head of account, the
Government stated that a request has been made before the Twelfth Finance Commission on 2.1.2003 to consider

States.  In making this proposal, the recommendation made by the Eleventh Finance Commission for creating Fast Track
Courts in various States was cited.
 
51.9.4  The Committee feels that the CBI should vigorously follow-up the matter with the Twelfth Finance Commission
and Action Taken thereon may be apprised to the Committee.
 
51.9.5  While pointing out the arrest of an officer of a Division of CBI i.e., Central Forensic Science Laboratory on account
of leakage of information, it was pointed out that in-house sabotage exists in the sensitive organization like CBI which
appeared to be one of the contributing factors for weakening its investigation. 
 
51.9.6  The Committee, therefore, desires that the Government may consider introduction of in-house surveillance system,
in CBI as exists in Intelligence Bureau (IB).

51.11.2 For filling the existing vacancies of investigating and legal officers, besides making vigorous efforts in calendar
year 2002 that did not yield much success, numerous options are being weighed.  Realizing that 106 vacant posts of DSPs
were affecting the functioning of the Bureau, 24 posts have been diverted from deputation to promotion quota, and the
proposal to consider promotion of eligible officers against these vacancies  is under consideration of the Union Public
Service Commission.  As regards the Annual Recruitment Plan, against the 43 Direct Recruitment posts of Legal Officers
and other categories in 'B', 'C' and 'D' levels, a meeting of the Screening Committee had been scheduled on 20.3.2003.

highest (44%) amongst investigating officers.

efficiency, through a simpler and quicker method may be worked out immedia

REPORT
CHAPTER -- I
Introductory
        The management of personnel policies in Government of India, to begin with, was the joint responsibility of the
Ministry of Home Affairs (Services and Establishment Wing) and Finance (Establishment Division) with Union Public
Service Commission playing an important advisory role. The Establishment Officer to the Government of India,
functioning under the Cabinet Secretary had an important role to play in the senior appointments under the Government
of India. All this made for improper division of responsibility and lack of a unified Central direction.
2.     To plug this organisation loophole, the Estimates Committee of the Third Lok Sabha in its 93 rd Report   (April
1966) observed that “the ever expanding role of the government in a welfare state with its natural concomitant of a large
civil service calls for effective personnel control through a single agency”.  The Administrative Reform Commission
(ARC) too urged upon the Government to set up a separate Department of Personnel with a full Secretary in charge, to
be placed directly under the Prime Minister to serve as a nodal agency for the personnel functions of the Government.
3.     The Union Government accepted this recommendation and as a consequence led to the reorganization of the
Ministry of Home Affairs as it then stood, resulting eventually in the formation of Ministry of Personnel, Public
Grievances and Pensions as it stands today. This process was initiated on June 26, 1970 when the Department of
Personnel was notified as a Department in the Cabinet Secretariat. The process was taken further on August 1, 1970
with the notification of the items of work to be dealt with by the Department of Personnel. Eventually, on March 15,
1985 a full fledged ‘Ministry of Personnel, Public Grievances and Pensions’ was notified.
4.0   The Ministry is the coordinating agency of the Central Government in personnel matters specially issues
concerning recruitment, promotion and morale of services, training, vigilance and discipline, career development and
service conditions of the senior middle management, grievances and staff welfare as well as the process of responsive
people-oriented modern administration. The Ministry comprises three Departments, namely: -
(i) Department of Personnel and Training.

99th report of Committee on HOME AFFAIRS
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Home%20Affairs/99threport.htm[30-06-2016 17:58:50]
(ii) Department of Pensions and Pensioners’ Welfare.
(iii) Department of Administrative Reforms and Public Grievances
.
4.1   The Ministry has under its administrative control three attached offices, namely: -
(i) Staff Selection Commission (SSC);
(ii) Institute of Secretariat Training and Management (ISTM); and
(iii) Lal Bahadur Shastri National Academy of Administration (LBSNAA).
4.2   The Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) was also an attached office under the administrative control of the
Ministry until the amendment in the Government of India (Allocation of Business) Rules, 1961, affected on 30 January
2003 thereby delinking the CBI from the Ministry of Personnel, Public Grievances and Pensions. The CBI is now under
the administrative control of Cabinet Secretariat.
4.3   The other offices under the administrative control of the Ministry are:-
(i) Union Public Service Commission (UPSC), a constitutional body;
(ii) Central Vigilance Commission (CVC), proposed to be converted into a statutory body;
(iii) Central Administrative Tribunal (CAT), a statutory quasi-judicial body; and
(iv) Public Enterprises Selection Board (PESB), a body set up by the resolution of Government.
5.     The Ministry is under the overall charge of the Prime Minister, assisted by a Minister of State. All the three
Departments are functioning under the charge of the Secretary (Personnel) assisted by one Special Secretary, three
Additional Secretaries and three Joint Secretaries and other supporting officers and staff.
DEPARTMENT OF PERSONNEL AND TRAINING AND THE VARIOUS AGENCIES UNDER ITS
ADMINISTRATIVE CONTROL
6.0   The role of the Department of Personnel and Training can be conceptually divided into two parts. In its larger
nodal role, it acts as the formulator of policy and the watchdog of the Government ensuring that certain accepted
standards and norms, as laid down by it, are followed by all Ministries/Departments in the recruitment, regulation of
service conditions and deputation of personnel as well as other related issues. Towards this end, guidelines are issued by
it for the benefit of all Ministries/Departments and it monitors the implementation of these guidelines. It also advises all
organisations of the Central Government on issues of personnel management. At a more immediate level, the
Department has the direct responsibility of being the cadre controlling authority for the Indian Administrative Service
(IAS) and the Central Secretariat Service (CSS). The Department also operates the Central Staffing Scheme under
which suitable officers from all India Services and Group ‘A’ Central Services are selected and then placed in posts at
the level of Deputy Secretary, Director and Joint Secretary on the basis of tenure deputation. The Department also deals
with cases of appointment to posts of Chairmen, Managing Directors, full-time functional Directors/Members of the
Board of Management of Various public sector undertakings/enterprises, corporations, banks and financial institutions.
It also deals with the assignment of Indian experts to various developing countries.
Recruitment Agencies
6.1   The two organisations through which the Department ensures recruitment of Personnel for the Government are the
Union Public Commission (UPSC) and the Staff Selection Commission (SSC). The former is constituted under a
provision of the Constitution and is responsible for conducting examinations for appointment to the higher civil services
and civil posts under the Union Government, including recruitment to the All India Services. There is a mandatory
provision for consulting the Commission on all matters relating to methods of recruitment, principles to be followed in
making promotions and transfers from one service to another and all the disciplinary matters. The SSC is responsible for
making recruitment for Group ‘B’ non-gazetted posts of Assistants, Stenographers, etc.
Training Institutions
6.2   Two major training institutions directly under the administrative control of the Department are the Lal Bahadur
Shastri National Academy of Administration (LBSNAA), Mussoorie and the Institute of Secretariat Training the
Management (ISTM), New Delhi. The former is mainly responsible for providing induction training to recruits to the
Indian Administrative Service and other All India Services and Central Services. The Institute of Training and
Management provides induction as well as in-service training to members of the Central Secretariat Service.
Senior Appointments under the Government of India
6.3   All proposals for senior appointments under the Government of India, which require the approval of the
Appointments Committee of the Cabinet (ACC) under the Government of India (Transaction of Business) Rules, 1961

are processed through the Establishment Officer as Secretary to the ACC. These include board level appointments to
Central Public Sector Undertakings and appointments of Joint Secretaries, Directors and Deputy Secretaries in the
Ministries/Departments. In addition, all appointments by promotion, which require the approval of the ACC are also
processed through the Establishment Officer.
Public Enterprises Selection Board (PESB)
6.4   The Public Enterprises Selection Board (PESB) is entrusted with the responsibility of making recommendations for
appointment to the full-time Board level posts of Chief Executive and functional Directors and part-time Chairman in
the Central Public Undertakings.
Administrative Vigilance
6.5   The Department of Personnel and Training determines Government policy for the maintenance of integrity of the
public services and eradication of corruption and coordinates the activities of various Ministries/Departments in that
area.
Central Vigilance Commission (CVC)
6.6   Advice on all vigilance matters is provided by the Central Vigilance Commission. It has jurisdiction and power in
respect of all matters to which the executive power of the Union Government extends. The Commission is also entrusted
with the supervision of the Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI). The Commission enjoys the same measure of
independence and autonomy as the Union Public Service Commission.
Joint Consultative Machinery
6.7   The Joint Consultative Machinery (JCM) is three-tier machinery consisting of the National Council, the
Departmental Council and the Regional/Office Council. Service matters pertaining to the interests of the generality of
employees or specific groups of them are dealt with by this machinery.
Central Administrative Tribunal (CAT)
6.8   In order to provide speedy and inexpensive justice to employees aggrieved by Government decisions, the
Government has set up the Central Administrative Tribunal (CAT) in 1985, which now deals with all cases relating to
service matters which were previously dealt with by Courts upto and including the High Courts.
Staff Welfare
6.9   The Department of Personnel and Training is intimately involved in several staff welfare and similar activities.
Mention in this connection can be made of the institution of Grih Kalyan Kendra (a society registered under the
Societies Registration Act, 1860), the Kendriya Bhandar (a registered cooperative society set up in 1963) and the
Central Civil Services Cultural and Sports Board (a society registered under the Societies Registration Act, 1860).
6.10 The Department also supports various programmes, which are provided in various Ministries/Departments, Central
Government Employees Welfare Coordination Committee in Central Government offices located outside Delhi,
Residents’ Welfare Associations/Area Welfare Officers, Benevolent Fund and Departmental Canteens.
DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND PENSIONERS’ WELFARE
7.0   The Department of Pension and Pensioners’ Welfare is the nodal agency of the Government of India for
formulation of general policy on pension and other retirement benefits, as also for redressal of grievances on retirement
benefits. The Department was set up in 1985 as a part of Ministry of personnel, Public Grievances and Pensions and has
been rendering service for the benefit of pensioners since then. The Department has taken a number of steps over the
years for streamlining the pension administration system, for greater convenience and welfare of the pensioners.
7.1   This Department, does not deal directly with pensioners but is the focal point for dealing with issues concerning
pensioners and for issue of instructions and guidelines regarding matters pertaining to pensioners.
7.2   The main responsibilities entrusted to this Department are:
          (i)    Formulation of policies and coordination of matters relating to retirement benefits of Central Govt.
employees including Defence and Railways;
          (ii)    Administration of
                 (a)   Central Civil Services (Pension) Rules, 1972;
                 (b)   Central Civil Services (Commutation of Pension) Rules, 1981;
                 (c)   Central Civil Services (Extraordinary Pensions) Rules;
                 (d)   General Provident Fund (Civil Services) Rules, 1960;
                 (e)   Deposit Linked Insurance Revised Scheme; and

DEPARTMENT OF ADMINISTRATIVE REFORMS AND PUBLIC GRIEVANCES
8.0   The Department of Administrative Reforms and Public Grievances is the nodal agency of the Government of India
for administrative reforms as well as redressal of public grievances relating to the State in general and grievances
pertaining to Central Government agencies in particular. The Department disseminates information on important
activities of the Government relating to administrative reforms and public grievance redressal through Management
Publications and Documentation. This Department also acts as the nodal agency in regard to Organisation an Methods
activities and offers advice to the Ministries/Departments. It also undertakes activities in the field of international co-
operation and exchanges to promote public service reforms.
8.1   This Department, has, in the last few years, taken several initiatives with a view to bring about improvement in the
functioning and effectiveness of Government Departments. To mention a few, the following are important ones:
          (i)    drawing up an agenda for reforms to be carried out in the Central Government as well as in States; and
          (ii)    undertaking through a Commission, a review of administrative laws which have become obsolete and no
longer need to be in the statute book.
8.2   The Department also initiated an exercise on the part of Departments having public interface to draw up their
individual Citizen’s charter to indicate the commitments of that organization for quality and the time-frame in which
services performed by that organization would be completed for members of the public.

Administration (IIPA), New Delhi. A decision has been taken to progressively reduce the grant-in-aid by 10% per year,
