reduced availability of funds. The decrease under this head is on account of the 10% reduction in the grant-in-aid
compared to the previous year.
13.2 The Committee notes the decision of the Government to make the Indian Institute of Public Administration
(IIPA) financially independent by gradually reducing its dependence on Government for funds. It also opines
that the Government should identify other institutions getting grants-in-aid and help those to gradually become
financially independent. However, the reduction of the grants-in-aid should not be dictated by the criterion of
non-availability of funds, rather by the capability of the institution in maintaining its financial requirements
independently.
14.0 To the query on what prompted the Ministry for making a sharp increase in the allocation under the minor head
“10.01.20” – ‘Other Administrative Expenses’ to the tune of Rs. 5.5 crore, the Ministry stated that the provision under
this minor head is used for implementing a UNDP assisted project called “Strengthening of the State Administrative
Training Institutes (ATIs)”. Provisions had to be made to enable a channelisation of the UNDP grant through the
budget. During 2002-2003, the Planning Commission had not taken the requirements of the UNDP assisted projects into
account in making the final outlay for the Ministry and had therefore made a provision of Rs. 1.33 crore out of the Rs. 9
crore requirement outlay projection of the Ministry to enable continuation of the project. The fixed term of the UNDP
project is done to end in December 2003. Consequently, an allocation of Rs. 5.5 crore has been sought to meet the cost
of the remaining work programme to be taken up during the year.

therefore recommends the proposed allocation of the Ministry.

DEMAND NO.-74 (UNION PUBLIC SERVICE COMMISSION)
21.0 The Union Public Service Commission is a constitutional body, created under Article 315 of the Constitution. The
Commission’s charter of duties is given in Article 320  and 321 of the Constitution. In brief, it is the duty of the
Commission to conduct examinations for appointment to services of the Union and to advise Government on all matter
relating to framing of recruitment rules, method of recruitment and the principle to be followed in making promotions
and transfers from one service to another. The Commission is also required to be consulted in respect of disciplinary
matters affecting a civil servant including appeals and memoranda filed by individual Government servants. The
Commission’s advice is also sought regarding any claim for reimbursement of legal proceedings instituted against him
for acts done in execution of his duties and on the question of award of pension for injury sustained by a Government
servant in a civil capacity. By virtue of the provisions made in the relevant Acts, the Commission is required to be
consulted in respect of appointments to certain categories of posts under the Municipal Corporation of Delhi, the
Employees’ State Insurance Corporation and the Employees’ Provident Fund Organization.
21.1 Article 322 of the Constitution envisages inter-alia  that expenses of the UPSC including salaries, allowances and
pensions payable to members and staff of the Commission shall be ‘charged’ on the Consolidated Fund of India. A

CHAPTER – III
POLICY, PROGRAMME AND SCHEMES OF THE MINISTRY
LAL BAHADUR SHASTRI NATIONAL ACADEMY OF ADMINISTRATION
22.0 The Lal Bahadur Shastri National Academy of Administration (LBSNAA) located at Mussoori in Uttaranchal is
primarily an institution for training of entrants to Government service through the annual Civil Service Examination
conducted by the UPSC. The responsibility is discharged by the Academy by means of a Foundational Course
conducted for the bulk of the different services covered by the Civil Services Examination, besides imparting intensive
and in-depth training to entrants to the Indian Administrative Service. The Academy also conducts programmes for in-
service training of IAS officers, including officers appointed to the IAS from State Civil Services. For other services
like the Indian Police Service (IPS), the Indian Revenue Service as well as the different Railway Services, the training

institutions are the National Police Academy at Hyderabad, the National Academy for Direct Taxes at Nagpur and the
Railway Staff College at Vadodara.
22.1 In so far as the Foundational Course for the All India and the Central Services is concerned, the objectives of this
course is given below:
           (a)    to promote esprit de corps among the probationers of different services, emphasizing the inter-dependence
of various services as part of the higher civil services;
           (b)   to motivate probationers towards developing certain basic professional, administrative and human values;
and
           (c)    to impart a basic understading of the constitutional, political, social, economic, legal, historical, cultural and
administrative framework within which the services function.
22.2 In addition to the induction and professional courses exclusively for IAS officers, the Academy also runs a large
number of short duration courses, from 2-3 days to two weeks period.
22.3 On being asked as to the number of short duration courses conducted by the Academy during the last three years,
the Government informed that in 2000, 19 courses were conducted where 542 participated, 17 courses in 2001 with 350
participation and 8 courses in 2002 with 172 participation. From a perusal of the details of cadre/service for whom it
was intended, it has been observed that out of the 44 courses 3 catered to services other than IAS and 20 courses catered
exclusively to the IAS while no mention was made with regard to 21 courses.
23.   The Committee taking note of the contribution made by the Lal Bahadur National Academy of Administration in
catering to the training needs of services other than the IAS, desires that the Academy should devise short-term in-house
departmental capsule courses for the new entrant officers in respective departments on a quarterly basis. Attending these
courses for all newly posted officers from the level of Under Secretary and above should be made mandatory. Similar
quarterly capsule courses should be devised for new entrants below rank of Under Secretary to impart complete
knowledge about the Department. The course content of the LBSNAA for the junior civil servants should include
subjects like agriculture. By incorporating the detailed knowledge of various departments to the departmental training
programmes, the LBSNAA could increase the time in the inputs for improving the agricultural contents in the
probationers course.
24.   The Committee has also been informed that due to non-clearance of sponsoring authority or for other reasons, the
number of participants actually attending the programme is less than the number of participants who have confirmed
their participation in the course. Besides, there is a sense of declining seriousness on part of the participants, perhaps
because their performance in the training programmes do not count for their promotion or find entry in the Annual
Confidential Reports (ACRs).
25.   The Committee taking note of the declining seriousness of the participants in the training programmes, feel that
this decline is perhaps more due to the lack of relevance to the actual job and as such the course contents should be
made relevant to his/her posting. Further, the training programmes for junior level officers should include components
on self-awareness and human values and inputs that would enable them to improve their basic attitude and have a better
understanding of ground level conditions. The Committee opines that such training programme should include
awareness of the Freedom of Information Act, 2002 for bringing in transparency in the administrative function of the
Government.
26.0 To a question with regard to the objectives and concerns of the training activities of the Academy, the Committee
has been informed that in addition to the objectives of imparting knowledge, developing skills and enhancing policy
formulation capabilities, the Academy also lays stress on bringing about right attitudinal orientation.
26.1 The Committee wanted to know whether training programme on ethics and values are conducted by the Academy.
The Government informed that the Academy conducts two courses of one-week duration each, every year on the theme
“Ethical values in Today’s Administration”. So far, the Academy has conducted seven such courses. The basic issues
dealt with the regarding ethical dilemmas in the Government. The Academy shares the concern that there is an erosion
of the humane aspects of administration. The Academy exposes the trainees to persons of eminence who can serve as
positive role models. Modules on “Self Awareness” and other training inputs like Team Building, Responsive
Administration and Sensitisation to the problems and needs of the people, especially those who belong to the poorer and
backward sections of the society, and Village visit are also conducted aimed at bringing about right attitudinal
orientation in the officer trainees.
26.2 The Ministry further stated that the objective of the programme is to expose the participants to the basic principles

of Ethics/Moral Philosophy; tease them into thinking about the values that underpin the framing and implementation of
public policy; and expose them to the ethical frameworks that policy makers use to resolve sticky public policy issues.
The aim is to create an atmosphere in which participatory learning takes place. A churning of the considerable
experience and knowledge of the participants through sharing and debate is encouraged not only to achieve the stated
objectives of the course but also to bring about a vertical integration of the group.
27.0 While appreciating the efforts of the Academy to imbibe ethics and positive values in the participants, the
Committee recommends that such training should be broad based to cater to maximum number of officers. It is of the
opinion that training programmes need to impart skills for interaction with the public in a humane manner.
27.1 The Committee feels that one of the major reasons for lack of interest especially in the foundation and probationary
courses, is the complacency the trainees have developed that all of them will inevitably be declared as passed. Trainees
who fail in various subjects are allowed to reappear at the next examination and the next and so on till eventually they
are declared as pass. The confirmation of services of those who fail in various subjects makes a mockery of the word
“probationer”. There is urgent need for Government to review their policy regarding probationers who fail in subjects
prescribed in the course. The Committee is of the view that probationers who fails to clear all the examinations set out
for them should be declared as failed and then services terminated. Only in proven cases where a probationer fails for
reasons beyond his control should he be permitted to appear just once more and if he fails again termination of his
service should be the rule.
PUBLIC ENTERPRISES SELECTION BOARD
28.0 Public Sector Enterprises (PSE) under the control of the Ministry of Personnel, Public Grievances and Pensions
play a vital role in the development of the national economy. In order to evolve a sound managerial personnel policy for
the Public Sector Enterprises and, in particular, to advise Government on appointments to the top management posts, the
Government of India constituted a Public Enterprises Section Board (PESB) by a Resolution dated 30 August 1974.
Consequent upon the shift of the secretariat of the PESB from the Department of Public Enterprises to the Department
of Personnel and Training from 9 July 1986, a comprehensive review of the policy relating to the functions,
membership, methodology for selection and infrastructure of the PESB was made by Resolution dated 3 March 1987 of
Ministry of Personnel, Public Grievances and Pensions. Amendments have been made to the Resolution from time to
time, the latest being made on 19 April 2000.
28.1 The PESB functions as a professional body with a large measure of autonomy. Its function are:
          (i)    to be responsible for the selection and placement of personnel in the posts of Chairman, Managing Director
or Chairman-cum-Managing Director (Level I), and Functional Director (Level II) in PSEs as well as in posts
at any other level as may be specified by the Government;
          (ii)   to advise the Government on matters relating to appointment, confirmation or extension of tenure an
termination of the services of personnel of the above mentioned levels;
          (iii)   to advise the Government on the desired structure at the Board level, and for senior management personnel,
for each PSE or group of PSEs;
          (iv)  to advise the Government on a suitable performance appraisal system for both the PSEs and the managerial
personnel in such enterprises;
          (v)   to build a data bank containing data relating to the performance of PSEs and its officers;
          (vi)  to advise the Government on formulation and enforcement of a Code of Conduct and Ethics for managerial
personnel in PSEs; and
          (vii) to advise the Government on evolving suitable training and development programmes for management
personnel in PSEs.
28.2   The PESB consists of one part-time or full-time Chairperson and three full-time Members. The Chairperson and
Members shall be persons who have had a long and distinguished career in management of public or private
corporations or public administration and have a proven record of achievements, preferably, in the field of personnel,
finance, production or marketing. The three full time members of the PESB shall be:
          (i)    A distinguished serving or former Chief Executive of a Public Sector or Private Sector or Joint Sector
Enterprise;
          (ii)   A distinguished person with experience in selection of top management personnel;

MODERNISATION OF GOVERNMENT OFFICES
30.   The Committee has been informed that modernization of any office must result in betterment of working
environment, increase in efficiency and should facilitate better flow of record and better delivery of services to the
public. Some of the othe attributes of modernized offices are as follows:---
          (a)   Optimal utilization of space by having a good functional lay out with modular furniture where files and
documents of current use are accessed easily.
          (b)   Storage facilities that have the appropriate size and shape which accommodate books/ledgers in the
Ministries/Departments.
          (c)   Provision of proper seating space for members of the public in public dealing sections and also free up staff
time by better record management so that the staff is able to look after public needs better.
          (d)   Proper seating arrangement to facilitate supervision.
          (e)   Providing suitable electric points to facilitate computerization.
31.0 The Committee is of the view that modernizing the entire administrative apparatus should not be an end in itself.
There should be an attitudinal change in the civil servants to serve the public at large. The Committee, therefore,
recommends that the Government should work out ways to imbibe attitudinal change in its personnel for better delivery
of services to the public.
31.1 The Committee also urges upon the Government to evolve clearly measurable parameters to assess the degree of
improvement made and also monitor those parameters on an effectively periodic basis.
NATIONAL INSTITUTE OF SMART GOVERNMENT
32.0 SMART is acronym for Simple, Moral, Accountable, Responsive and Transparent. The Ministry has initiated
several measures towards achieving the goal of operationalising SMART administration. The conference of Chief
Minister held in New Delhi on 29 May 1997 represented the culmination of the National Debate on Effective and
Responsive Administration. The Action Plan prepared for the Conference dealt with three themes, namely, making
administration accountable and citizen-friendly, ensuring transparency and Right to Information and taking measures to
cleanse and motivate Civil Services. The following are the major components of the aforesaid action plan, which are
also being operationalised:---
          (i)   Citizen’s Charter;
          (ii)   Information and Facilitation Counters (IFCs);
          (iii)  Redress of Public Grievance;
          (iv)  Review of Laws, Regulations and Procedures;
          (v)  Transparency in Government and Right to Information; and
          (vi)  A minimum Agenda for e-governance.

32.1 The National Institute for Smart Government (NISG) aims to be the premier enabler of ‘smart governance’ wherein
Governments’ knowledge, services and processes are conveniently accessible to its customers and designed around their
needs. In doing so, NISG intends to offer unique value proposition to six groups that define its existence; Citizens,
Governments, financial institutions, alliance partners that include IT firms, employees and stakeholders.
32.2 An amount to the tune of Rs. 2 crore in 2002-2003 was allocated for setting up of National Institute of Smart
Government (NISG). To a question as to why the allocation has not been utilised, the Government stated that the
Integrated Finance Division (IFD) had advised the Department to get the approval of the Cabinet as per the revised
instructions on the subject. They also raised some issues relating to funding pattern for setting up of NISG and the
Planning Commission to whom a reference was made for release of one crore also raised few issues on the same lines.
Since the funding pattern itself was based on the Business Plan approved by the High Powered Committee, it was
decided to place this matter before the High Powered Committee to obtain its views on the comments of Planning
Commission and IFD.
33.0 The Committee views that delay in execution of plan schemes defeat the purpose of the scheme. It, therefore,
recommends that the Ministry should follow up its proposal with the Cabinet and Planning Commission and make the
National Institute of Smart Government (NISG) functional.
GOOD GOVERNANCE
34.0 Accountability has become the worst casualty because the officers who are to enforce accountability are being
increasingly marginalized in the choice of appointing their subordinates to various posts, specially in the field which is
the cutting edge vis-a-vis the people. Responsibility and rights are inseparable. There is need to restore the rights of the
executive to enable it to discharge its responsibility regarding making itself accountable.
34.1 To a query posed by the Committee with regard to the specific areas/issues identified, the Government gave the
reply that in order to bring about good governance, the areas/issues identified includes – (i) review of administrative
laws; (ii) formulation of Citizen’s charters by the Central Ministries/Departments as also by State Governments; (iii)
setting up of Information and Facilitation Counters in the Ministries/Departments for easy and hassle free access of
information by the citizen; (iv) strengthening the public Grievance Redress Mechanism which is in place in various
Ministries/Departments of the Central Government; (v) implementation of a minimum agenda for promotion of e-
governance for re-engineering of various processess with a view to ensure quicker delivery of public services; and (vi)
documentation and dissemination of best practices in the area of administrative reforms.
35.   The Committee is of the view that with the help of e-governance, computers, improvement of information
technology, Freedom of Information and Citizen’s Charters, collection of basic data and information available with the

41.0 The Department of Administrative Reforms and Public Grievances coordinates the efforts to formulate and
operationalise citizen’s/user’s charter by the Central Government Ministries/Departments and their
PSUs/autonomous/statutory bodies in areas in which they provide services to the members of the public. The
Department also coordinates the efforts of formulating and operationalising Citizen’s Charter in various States/UTs.
41.1 The Committee has been informed that 19 Ministries/Departments have brought out 79 Citizen’s Charters.
Similarly, 23 organizations of the State Governments/UT Administrations have brought out 498 Citizen’s   Charters. 4
Regional Seminars on Citizen’s Charter were organized in 2001-2002 at Hyderabad, Mussoorie, Bhopal and Guwahati

State Governments/UT Administrations and 15 Central Government Ministries/Departments/Organizations participated

43.0 Information and Facilitation Counter (IFC) is the visible face/physical manifestation of Citizen’s Charter

43.1 Computerised Information and Facilitation Counters have been set up in various
Ministries/Departments/Organisations, etc. of the Government of India to provide information and assistance to the

43.2 To a query as to how many IFCs have been set up by Ministries/Departments/Organisations, the Ministry informed

46.   The Committee feels that there is need for publicity (India wide) through Doordarshan to enable the rural folk to
know about the existence of these two channels for the redressal of public grievances. Secondly in some cases the
replies received by the aggrieved do not provide solace and redressal expected from the grievance redressal mechanism
of the Government. The output, it is felt cannot reach the desired level without putting an effective Department-wise
monitoring mechanism that studies the measurable parameters which show tangible results.
47.
   Among various other measures taken by the Government to strengthen the grievance redress mechanism, a uniform
software called Public Grievance Redress and Monitoring System has been installed in 22 Ministries/Departments and
13 other organizations. The internet version of this system was launched on 31.05.2002

48.   The Committee, while taking note of the above measures to strengthen the grievance mechanism, recommends that
all out efforts should be made to effectively monitor the same and due attention should be given to timely redressal of
grievances lodged. It is also of the considered view that officers responsible for brooking delay should be made
accountable and suitable action taken against them. This mechanism may bring some success to computer savvy public,
but the bulk of India lives in villages. It is therefore that stress has been laid for evolving a mechanism that would serve
the less literates. The Committee expresses a desire to see the results of one such monitoring of each Department.

51.0 Pursuant to the provision of Article 323A of the Indian Constitution, the Administrative Tribunals Act, 1985 was
enacted by Parliament to set up Administrative Tribunal for adjudication of disputes and complaints with regard to
recruitment and condition of services of persons appointed to public services and posts in connection with the affairs of
the Union and the States.
51.1 Administrative adjudication, which is quasi-judicial in nature, is the main function of Administrative Tribunals.
The basic objective of enacting the Administrative Tribunal Act was:
          (i)    to relieve congestion in the ordinary set of courts; and
          (ii)    to provide for speedy disposal of disputes relating to service matters.
51.2 The Central Administrative Tribunals Act, 1985 provides that the Tribunal shall not be bound by the procedure laid
down in the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 but shall be guided by the principle of natural justice and subject to the other
provisions of Administrative Tribunals Act and rules made by the Central Government. The Tribunal shall have power
to regulate its own procedure including the fixing of places and times of enquiry. As a result of the judgement of the
Supreme Court in the case of L. Chandra Kumar dated 18 March 1997, the appeals against the orders of an
Administrative Tribunals lie before the Division Bench of the concerned High Court.
51.3 Administrative Tribunals are distinguishable from the ordinary Courts with regard to their jurisdiction and
procedure. They are free from the shackles of many of the technicalities of the ordinary Courts. The litigant(s) has to
submit an application in paper book form prescribed by rule 4 of Central Administrative Tribunal (Procedure) Rules,
1985. It means that every application should be accompanied by a proper containing the following:-
          (i)    Certified copy of the order against which the application has been filed;
          (ii)    All documents relied upon by the applicants and mentioned in the application;
          (iii)   Details of the crossed Demand Draft or crossed Indian Postal Order representing the application fee of Rs.
50/-; and
          (iv)   Index of documents.
        The aggrieved person can appear before the Court personally. Government can also present its case through its
Departmental officers or legal practitioners.
51.4 The Tribunal consists of a sanctioned strength of one Chairman, 16 Vice-Chairmen and 49 Members. The
Members are drawn from both judicial as well as administrative streams so to give the Tribunal the benefit of expertise
both in legal and administrative spheres.
51.5 The Committee, in its 87th Report on Demands for Grants (2002-2003) of the Ministry had recommended that the
process of selection of persons to fill up vacancies in the CAT should be initiated at least three months before its
occurrence to avoid a vacuum in the Tribunals. The Government had in its reply stated that the selection processes are
conducted in advance. However, due to litigation of some other unavoidable norms, the selection process is held up.
51.6 To a query regarding the present position of vacancies in the CAT, the Government informed that 4 posts of Vice-
Chairman and 10 posts of Administrative members are laying vacant in various Benches of CAT.

last date of receipt of candidatures on 10.3.2003. It has also been further stated that meeting of the Selection Committee

enumerated in clauses (a), (c), (d), (e) & (f) of Para 59.2. That being the case, the Committee has grave doubts if the
measures contemplated will at all make any dent on the problem of delays.

basis, the Committee has the following to suggest:
As each case of punishment has its own unique complexities, it is therefore suggested that in the light of the
complexities of each case which would be apparent to the CVC before it tenders the first stage advise, the CVC
must prescribe specific time frames with dates by which Ministries/Departments/Organisations must report to the
CVC about the implementation of CVC’s first stage advice. The same should be done in respect of the second
stage advice. If the Ministries/Departments/Organisations find that the time frame prescribed by the CVC is
impractical, they themselves must inform the CVC within seven days of the receipt of the advice as to the date by
which they shall be able to report the said implementation. If, thus the Ministries/Departments/Organisations fail to
keep up to their own suggested dates, the CVC should report to the head of the Department for taking action
against the dealing officer for inability to abide by his own date. Initially, warnings to such officers should be
placed on their personal files but if his performance does not improve even after three warnings, major punishment
proceedings should be initiated against that officer for incompetent handling of his duties. The Committee believes
that the root of the problem of delays lies in the absence of accountability of the dealing officers of the CVC, and
the dealing officers of the Ministries/Departments/Organisations and it is here where the action should commence
forthwith.
60.2 In the Meanwhile, the Committee, in consultation with the Ministry and the CVC shall in due course evolve a
permanent operational procedure.

various Court judgements. Fifth Central Pay Commission Report and the Study Reports of 1990 and 1994 prepared by
the Department of Administrative Reforms and Public Grievances in October 1998.
61.3 To a questions as to how far the scheme has served the welfare of the Government employees whose near relations
have opted for compassionate appointment, the Ministry has stated that the scheme for compassionate appointment
provides for compassionate appointments in Group ‘C’ and ‘D’ posts to the extent of 5% of the vacancies to be filled by
direct recruitment in Group ‘C’ and ‘D’ posts. It is further stated that the compassionate appointment is to be granted
only in most deserving cases to save the dependent family of a deceased/medically retired Government employees from
financial destitution. The Ministry has stated that the Scheme has its utility as a welfare measure.
62.0 Certain other specific questions had been put to the Ministry Viz.
          (a)   How far has the scheme served the welfare of Government employees ?
          (b)   Whether the implementation of the scheme was ever monitored to assess the extent to which families of
Government employees have been benefited and what are the details of such assessment?
          (c)   Whether the Ministry has ever collected data as to the number of deserving families that could not be helped
under this scheme ?
          (d)   Whether any Court Judgement/Order has defined what is “a family in penury”?
          (e)   Whether any supplementary guidelines defining “indigent conditions” were issued?
          (f)    Did the original scheme envisage the maintaining of a waiting list? What is the period of validity of such
waiting lists?
          (g)   As per the scheme, if the entire 5% vacancies are full in one Ministry/Department, whether appointment on
compassionate grounds could be made in any other Government of India Ministry/Department? Accordingly,
was any waiting list monitored to enable their accommodation in other Departments?
          (h)   How many cases on the waiting list of one Department were accommodated in other Departments during the
preceding 10 years?
          (i)    Whether calculation of 5% vacancies was affected by the ban on fresh recruitments? Has it meant a reduction
or is the 5% being calculated on the basis of the original sanctioned strength?
          (j)    Was there any time bar for compassionate appointments under this scheme?
          (k)   Whether the dependants of the deceased employees were permitted to retain Government accommodation in
anticipation of compassionate appointments?
          (l)    Whether the Ministry deems fit to consider giving a Group ‘D’ post to an applicant of Group ‘C’ post to
reduce the distress of the family?
          (m)  Whether DPOT or the Directorate of Estate prescribes any time limit regarding retention of the Government
Accommodation by family of the deceased employee? If so, what is that time limit?
62.1
 The responses of the Ministry to the afore-mentioned questions are not satisfactory. The committee feels that the
matter of compassionate appointments requires detailed discussion to formulate its
views/suggestions/recommendations. The Committee, therefore, requests the Ministry to furnish clear-cut answers
to the afore-mentioned questions within six weeks time from the date of presentation of its Report of Parliament to
enable it to hold discussion on the subject.

CHAPTER I
INTRODUCTORY
1.1 The Ministry of Urban Development & Poverty Alleviation has
been bifurcated into two separate Ministries viz. Ministry of Urban
Development and the Ministry of Urban Employment and Poverty
Alleviation w.e.f. 27th May, 2004. Ministry of Urban Employment and
Poverty Alleviation is entrusted with the responsibility of broad policy
formulation and monitoring of programmes and schemes in the areas
of housing and urban poverty alleviation. Poverty, for the most part
takes the shape of misery and deprivation among individuals and
households from security, fulfilment of survival needs and quality life.
In an environment where the poor are exploited and ignored, there is
major role for the States and its agencies including the Urban Local
Bodies (ULBs) in finer urban governance and urban development. The
Ministry of Urban Employment & Poverty Alleviation basically deals
with the following areas of concern:
(i) Formulation of housing policy and programme (except rural
housing), which is assigned to the Department of Rural
Development, review of the implementation of the Plan
schemes, collection and dissemination of data on housing,
building materials and techniques, general measures for
reduction of building costs and nodal responsibility for
National Housing Policy;
(ii) Human Settl ements including the United Nations
Commission for Human Settlements and International
Cooperation and Technical Assistance in the field of Housing
and Human Settlements;
(iii) Urban Development including Slum Clearance Schemes and
the Jhuggi and Jhonpri Removal Schemes. International
Cooperation and Technical Assistance in this field;
(iv) National Cooperative Housing Federation;
(v) Implementation of the specific programmes of Urban
Employment and Urban Poverty Alleviation including other
programmes evolved from time to time; and

2
(vi) All matters relating to the Housing and Urban Development
Corporation (HUDCO) other than those relating to urban
infrastructure.
1.2 The Ministry implements the above work through formulation
of appropriate policies, implementation of specific Plan programmes
of Housing and generation of employment in urban areas, and
supporting autonomous bodies for undertaking relevant programmes
and schemes.
1.3 The Planned Programmes supported by this Ministry comprise
of the Centrally Sponsored Schemes and Central Schemes. The Centrally
Sponsored Schemes are: (i) Swarna Jayanti Shahari Rozgar Yojana
(SJSRY); (ii) Valmiki Ambedkar Awas Yojana (VAMBAY); (iii) Integrated
Low Cost Sanitation Scheme for Liberation of Scavengers (ILCS);
(iv) National Scheme for Liberation and Rehabilitation of Scavengers
and their dependents (NSLRS); (v) Scheme for provision of
Infrastructure facilities in displaced persons urban colonies in West
Bengal; (vi) Night Shelter Schemes; and (vii) Building Centers; The
Central Schemes are: (i) Building Materials and Technology Promotion
Council (BMPTC); (ii) National Cooperative Housing Federation
(NCHF); (iii) Central Government Employees Welfare Housing
Organization (CGEWHO); (iv) United Nations Center for Human
Settlements (UNCHS); (v) National Building Organization (NBO);
(vi) Urban Indictors Programme.
Urban Reforms Incentive Fund (URIF)
1.4 During the year 2002-2003, the Government had set up a fund
named ‘Urban Reforms Incentive Fund’ (URIF) to provide reform linked
assistance to States as part of the Central assistance to State Plan.
Consequently, in addition to Centrally Sponsored Schemes and Central
Schemes, the Ministry also administers URIF. Funds are released for
URIF as Additional Central Assistance to Annual Plan of States by
Ministry of Finance on the basis of recommendations made by the
Ministry of Urban Employment and Poverty Alleviation.
1.5 Budget of the Ministry of Urban Employment and Poverty
Alleviation comprises of one Demand for Grants, i.e. Demand No.
103-Ministry of Urban Employment and Poverty Alleviation.

2.11 The Committee note from the Budget allocations that the

and ULBs for the implementation of a programme thereby defeating

7

that comprehensive monitoring should be done at the Central level
and periodical and timely review of the functioning of the
programmes under implementation should be made by a high level
body of the Ministry of Urban Employment & Poverty Alleviation
so as to ensure proper implementation of the schemes. The
Committee also recommend that concrete steps must be taken to
obviate incidences of rush hour spending or release of funds towards
the fag end of a financial year so that the allocated budgetary funds
are utilized constructively. The Ministry should chalk out a time-
frame regarding releases of funds under the Centrally Sponsored
Scheme of their Ministry to States/UTs.

CHAPTER III
URBAN POVERTY ALLEVIATION PROGRAMMES
Urban Poverty Alleviation
3.1 As per the 10th Five Year Plan document of the Planning
Commission, the number of urban unemployed in the country for
1999-2000 was 7.11 million, i.e. 7.65% of the labour force. The number
of persons living below the poverty line in urban areas is estimated
to be 67.1 million, i.e. 23.62% of the total urban population. As per the
Poverty Estimates prepared by the Planning Commission, the National
average per capita income defining the Poverty line for the urban
areas, as in 1999-2000, Rs. 454.11 per month. In order to combat poverty
in the country, the 10th Five Year Plan has targeted a reduction of
poverty ratio by 5 percentage points by 2017 and by 15 percentage
points by 2012.
3.2 In order to tackle the massive problem of unemployment/
poverty a multipronged strategy has to be formulated with more
schemes with adequate financial allocations and their effective
implementation. As per the 10th Plan document the implementation of
programme for the urban poor is beset with enormous problems. The
problem of inadequate funding has been compounded by under-
utilisation of Central funds, diversion of funds released for specific
programmes, and infructuous expenditure. Monitoring at the Central
level has been weak and ineffective. Success stories have not been
publicised or adopted on a wider scale. The understanding of the
programme, their objective and modalities relating to implementation
has been weak and superficial, leading to inaction in many areas that
are of vital concern to the urban poor. There are few master plans and
very little effort at monitoring the benefits that are expected to flow
to the target communities. In addition, there has been too much
emphasis on engineering or the works aspects of programmes without
adequate understanding of the social, psychological and other dynamics
of poverty. Many a times even the beneficiaries have not been consulted
nor given a voice in the implementation of programmes.
3.3 When asked about the success of the Government in alleviation
of poverty in realistic terms, the Ministry of Urban Employment &
Poverty Alleviation in a written note has stated that in 1993-94, the
8

9
urban poverty ratio was 32.4% and it came down to 23.6% in
1999-2000 i.e. a decrease of 8.8%. This decrease in poverty ratio can
inter-alia, be attributed to the impact and effective implementation of
the various urban poverty alleviation programmes of the Government.
3.4 Regarding this vital question of eradication of urban poverty
and the growing volume of urban unemployment in the country and
the mode to confront this misery, the Ministry of Urban Employment
& Poverty Alleviation have informed the Committee that the Ministry
of Urban Employment Poverty Alleviation is implementing an urban
poverty alleviation scheme named Swarna Jayanti Shahari Rozgar
Yojana on all India basis. Taking into consideration the availability of
funds under the Scheme, including the unspent balances from earlier
poverty alleviation schemes, in the 10th Plan (2000-07) a target to
provide 4 lakh self employment opportunities and 5 lakh skill
upgradation opportunities to the BPL persons has been fixed. In
addition, under Wage Employment component of the Scheme, there is
a provision to provide wage employment to the BPL population.
3.5 On a question of adequacy of funds allocated for the
employment and poverty alleviation programmes including the
allocation of Rs. 830 crore for 2004-2005 for urban employment and
poverty alleviation to solve the problem urban poor in this area, the
Ministry in the written reply has stated that the allocation of Rs. 830
crore for 2004-05 is for all the schemes implemented by the Ministry
of Urban Employment & Poverty Alleviation and SJSRY is the urban
poverty alleviation programme and the allocated funds are inadequate
to meet the requirement of the urban poor population of 67.1 million.
3.6 The Committee note that in 1993-94, the urban poverty ratio
was 32.4% and it came down to 23.6% in 1999-2000 i.e. a decrease of
8.8%. The Committee are, however, not at all convinced by the stand
taken by the Ministry that this decrease in poverty ratio is attributed
to the impact and effective implementation of the various urban
poverty alleviation programmes of the Government as they are of
the firm view that the Government have yet to go a long way in
tackling the problem of poverty alleviation and effective
implementation of schemes/programmes earmarked for upliftment
of the urban poor population. The Committee endorse the observation
made in the 10th Plan Document that the implementation of
programmes for the urban poor is beset with enormous problems
and the problem of inadequate funding has been compounded by
under-utilisation of Central funds, diversion of funds released for

10
specific programmes, and infructuous expenditure. The Committee,
therefore, recommend that concerted efforts be made by the Central
as well as the State Governments in line with the planned objectives
of poverty eradication by way of efficient monitoring at the Central
level and involvement of State level coordinators, urban local bodies
and NGOs.
3.7 The Committee note that the Ministry’s contention is that
the funds allocated to the poverty alleviation scheme are inadequate
to meet the requirements of about 67.1 million urban poor population.
In this respect, the Committee would like to emphasize that ongoing
poverty and employment schemes should be fully and effectively
implemented at first in the States and periodic and timely monitoring
of the schemes should be carried out at Central level. The Committee
are also of the firm view that appropriate punitive measures must
be taken at the Ministerial level in cases where misuse and diversion
of funds has come to the notice. The Committee would like to be
apprised of the steps taken in this direction at the earliest.
Allocation for North-Eastern Region including Sikkim

2001 that 10% of the total budget provision for the Ministries/

(i) Housing projects (predominantly for the urban poor)

1. Swarna Jayanti Shahari Rozgar Yojana (SJSRY)
3.13 Swarna Jayanti Shahari Rozgar Yojana (SJSRY) was launched
on 01.12.1997 after subsuming the earlier three Urban Poverty
Alleviation Schemes, namely Urban Basic Services for the Poor (UBS),
Nehru Rojgar Yojana (NRY) and Prime Ministers Integrated Urban
Poverty Eradication Programme (PMIUPEP), with a view to provide
gainful employment to the urban unemployed or underemployed
through encouraging the setting up of self-employment ventures or
provision of wage employment. This programme relies on creation of
suitable community structures and delivery of inputs is through the
medium of urban local bodies and such community structure. The
SJSRY is funded on 75:25 basis between Centre and States.
3.14 This programme targets the urban poor, as those living below
the urban poverty line, as defined from time to time by the Planning
Commission.
Salient Features of SJSRY
3.15 Swarna Jayanti Shahari Rozgar Yojana (SJSRY) consists of two
major components, namely:
(a) The Urban Self Employment Programme (USEP)
(b) The Urban Wage Employment Programme (UWEP)

13
The Urban Self Employment Programme (USEP)
3.16 The salient features of this component are:
(i) Assistance to individual urban poor beneficiaries for setting
up gainful self-employment ventures;
(ii) Assistance to groups of urban poor women for setting up
gainful self-employment ventures. This sub-scheme has been
titled as “The Scheme for Development of Women and
Children in the Urban Areas (DWCUA)”
(iii) Training of beneficiaries, potential beneficiaries and other
persons associated with the urban employment programme
for upgradation and acquisition of vocational and
entrepreneurial skills;
(iv) Special attention is given to women, person belonging to
Scheduled Castes/Tribes, disabled persons and other such
categories as may be indicated by the Government from
time to time;
(v) The percentage of women beneficiaries under this
programme should not be less than 30%. All other conditions
being equal, women beneficiaries belonging to women-
headed household, viz. widows, divorcees, single women or
even households, where women are the sole earners, are
ranked higher in priority. SCs and STs must be benefited at
least to the extent of the proportion of their strength in
local population. A provision of 3% should be reserved for
the disabled;
(vi) There is no minimum educational qualification for
beneficiaries under this programme. However, this scheme
is not applicable to the persons educated beyond the IXth
standard;
(vii) A house-to-house survey for identification of genuine
beneficiaries is prescribed. Non-economic parameters are also
applied to the urban poor in addition to the economic
criteria for the purpose of prioritization within the BPL;
(viii) Setting up Micro-Enterprises with maximum unit cost of
Rs. 50,000 and Skill Development of beneficiaries and to
provide training and infrastructure support; and

14
(ix) Development of women and Children in Urban Areas
(DWCUA) by encouraging the women to take up Self-
Employment.
The Urban Wage Employment Programme (UWEP):
3.17 (i) This component seeks to provide wage employment to
prospective beneficiaries living below the poverty line within
the jurisdiction of urban local bodies by utilising their labour
for construction of socially and economically useful public
assets;
(ii) This programme applies to the urban local bodies having
population less than 5 lakh as per the 1991 Census;
(iii) The material labour ratio for works under this component
is to be maintained at 60:40. The prevailing minimum wage
rate, as notified from time to time for each area, has to be
paid to beneficiaries under this component;
(iv) This programme is dovetailed with the State Sector EIUD
scheme as well as the NSDP . This programme is not
designed to either replace or substitute the EIUS, the NSDP ,
or any other State Sector schemes.
Information, Education and Communication (IEC) and Community
Structure Components.
3.18 With a view to playing an effective role in coordination and
in organising training, monitoring, evaluation, dissemination of
information etc. a new component of IEC has been evolved under
SJSRY. It is proposed to have a coordinated and uniform level of
training across the country for training of trainers, elected
representatives, functionaries of Urban Local Bodies and field
functionaries like Project Officers, Community Organisers etc. through
National Training Institutes and selected State Training/Field Training
Institutes.
3.19 Under SJSRY, Community Structure is created in all the urban
towns of the country. The State Governments have taken action to set
up community structure, create Community Development Societies
(CDSs) and form Thrift & Credit Society etc.

However, this Scheme is not applicable to the persons educated

22
3.42 The Committee feel that as per the guidelines, the higher
education beyond 9th Standard acts as an disincentive to urban poor
as he is not entitled to avail of the benefits of the Scheme. The
Committee feel that there is a need to review the said condition.
The benefit under the scheme should be available to urban poor
irrespective of his educational qualification so that more and more
young poor can come forward and by getting the benefits of the
Scheme cross the poverty line.
3.43 The Committee note that the erstwhile Nehru Rozgar Yojana
meant to provide employment to poor urban youth was restructured
as SJSRY. The Committee conclude from what has been stated above
that there are serious problems being faced in the implementation
of the Scheme as has been admitted by the Ministry itself. There is
no proper monitoring mechanism, Union Government is dependent
upon the State Governments for monitoring. Further, even the survey
for identification of beneficiaries that is the first stage of
implementation is underway. Beyond this there is the problem of
non-cooperation of Banks. The Committee feel that at the field level
there are certain type of problems viz. huge gap between the number
of applicants and the sanction and disbursement of loan, the
applications are rejected on flimsy ground. All the issues related to
the Banks should be sorted out after interaction with the Ministry
of Finance, RBI and the concerned Banks. There should be a
mechanism to hold the regular meetings with RBI and Banks and
the necessary follow-up action should be taken to make the
programme effective. Not only that there is a need to improve the
delivery mechanism of the Scheme through augmenting training and
proper monitoring. Further stress should be on Self Help Groups by
providing them forward and backward linkages. The Ministry should
think of providing better market facilities to enable SHGs to sell
their products. Besides, the products made by SHGs should be sold
through various Shilp Melas like Saras being organized at Delhi
International Trade Fair. Such melas should be organized in other
big cities also of the country. Besides, like Delhi Haat, in other
cities too such Haats should be opened and the products produced
by SHGs should be sold. Wide publicity should also be given to
the products produced by the SHGs so as to encourage them. Another
area of concern is to make the products produced by Self Help
Groups (SHGs) competitive. There is a need to provide training to
improve the quality of the products. More and more NGOs should
be involved in the task. SHGs should be involved in the trade
according to the local needs of the area where these are manufactured

23
so as to ensure the viability of SHGs. Once SHGs are viable and
are engaged in profit making activity, there will not be any problem
of Bank loan. Banks would come forward themselves to provide
loan under the Scheme. In view of the aforesaid position there is an
urgent need to take all the corrective steps as given above so as to
make the programme more effective.
2. Valmiki Ambedkar Awas Yojana (V AMBAY)
3.44 With a purpose to provide shelter or upgrade the existing
shelter for people living below poverty line in urban slums in a march
towards the goal of slumless cities with a healthy and enabling urban
environment, a new Centrally Sponsored Scheme called Valmiki
Ambedkar Awas Yojana (VAMBAY) was launched during the year 2001-
2002 in accordance with the announcement made by the Hon’ble Prime
Minister on 15th August, 2001. The target group under VAMBAY is all
slum-dwellers in urban areas, who are below the poverty line including
members of EWS, who do not possess adequate shelters. Nirmal Bharat
Abhiyan is an integral component of VAMBAY for construction of
community toilets and sanitation. The funding pattern under VAMBAY
would be 50:50 basis between the Central and State Governments.
Financial allocation
3.45 Valmiki Ambedkar Awas Yojana (VAMBAY) was formally
launched on 02.12.2001 with a budget provision of Rs. 69.00 crore
provided out of the savings of the Departmental budget during the
year 2001-2002. However, a sum of Rs. 73.56 crore was finally released
out of the savings of the Departmental budget during the year 2001-
2002.
3.56 In the 10th Plan Rs. 2040 crore have been allocated for the
scheme. The detail of financial allocation during the last three years is
as under:
2002-2003 Rs. 256.85 crore
2003-2004 Rs. 238.50 crore
2004-2005 Rs. 280.58 crore

1,00,000) and 21,488 community toilets. However, 15% of the allocated

24
amount could not be utilised due to non-receipt of proposals, complete
in all respects, from the State Governments in some of the components
of VAMBAY though in shelter component the demand was enough to
utilise all the allotted amount. The request for re-appropriation of funds
from other components of VAMBAY to the shelter component was
taken up with Ministry of Finance. They however, did not agree to

3.48 In the year 2003-2004, an amount of Rs. 238.55 crore was

3.49 When enquired about the major components of VAMBAY
where demands were not enough to utilise all the allotted amount the

Target

25
Monitoring/Evaluation

through regular review meetings at Secretary/Joint Secretary levels with

HUDCO have also been formed which have started visiting the States
for overseeing the implementation of the programme. The Government

Coordination Committee (SLCC) for monitoring the implementation of
VAMBAY at the State Level.
3.54 When asked about the details of the work done so far by the
Core Group for overseeing the implementation of the Scheme the
Ministry in a reply has stated that initially Core Groups were formed
in HUDCO to oversee the implementation of VAMBAY in the States
where projects were being implemented. However, orders were issued
by the Ministry formally for constitution of State Level Co-ordination
Committees (SLCC) comprising State Government/agency officials,

progress of VAMBAY scheme in the States.
3.55 The Committee note that main purpose behind V AMBAY
scheme is to provide shelter or upgrade the existing shelter for BPL
persons living in urban slums of the country. This scheme, launched
in 2001-2002 has been allocated funds amounting to Rs. 2,040 crore
in the Tenth Plan period. The financial allocation in 2002-2003
amounted to Rs. 256.85 crore and in 2003-2004 the allocation was to
the tune of Rs. 238.50 crore. Out of the total allocation of Rs. 256.85
crore for the year 2002-2003 under V AMBAY, central subsidy of
Rs. 218.35 crore was released for construction of 1,10,388 dwelling
units (more than the target set i.e. 1,00,000) and 21,488 community
toilets. However, 15% of the allocated amount could not be utilised
due to non-receipt of proposals from the State Governments in some
of the components of V AMBAY though in shelter component, the
demand was enough to utilise all the allotted amount. In such
circumstances, the Committee cannot but express their distress about
the sorry state of affairs of implementation of the V AMBAY scheme.
The Committee are compelled to re-emphasise that the delivery
mechanism of the Ministry needs to be really beefed up in
coordination with the concerned State Governments and ULBs. The
Committee recommend that an accountable system of checks should
be chalk out so as to ensure timely release of funds and full
implementation of V AMBAY programme. The Committee would like
to be apprised about the steps taken in this regard in due course.

26
3.56 The Committee find that V AMBAY was started in the
year 2001. They note that under Nirmal Abhiyan Component of
V AMBAY, sufficient demand was not received during 2002-2003 and
2003-2004. The Committee note that almost three years have elapsed
since the Scheme was started. The Ministry should review the various
components of the Scheme in consultation with State Governments
and Urban Local Bodies so that projections for the different
components of V AMBAY can be made. After a review of various
components and after proper analysis the Government should revise
the guidelines.
3.57 The Committee are contented to note that V AMBAY being
a demand driven scheme, a target of construction of 1.12 lakh
dwelling units has been set internally by Ministry for the current
financial year 2004-2005. The Committee are of the firm view that it
is essential to have a target for achieving as well as assessment of
implementation of a scheme like V AMBAY which is the only scheme
for providing shelter or upgrading the existing shelter for slum
dwellers in urban slums.
3.58 The Committee note that under V AMBAY Central subsidy
is granted for construction of dwelling unit @Rs. 20,000 for general
cities, Rs. 25,000 for Metro Cities and Rs. 30,000 for mega cities.
Some States like Karnataka, Madhya Pradesh etc. have requested to
enhance the existing cost of construction/central subsidy of a dwelling
unit. The Committee have been given to understand that the funding
pattern under V AMBAY between Central and State Governments is
on 50:50 basis. In regard to unit cost of dwelling unit as given
above, the Committee are of the opinion that meaningful amount of
Central subsidy should be granted to the State Governments for
construction of dwelling units keeping in view the current market
prices and cost of construction involved in the units. The Committee,
therefore, recommend that comprehensive State-wise assessment of
escalation of cost of construction of units under the V AMBAY scheme
should be made and the central subsidy for V AMBAY projects be
enhanced, accordingly.
3.59 The Committee note that initially Core Groups were formed
in HUDCO to over-see the implementation of V AMBAY in the States

27
where projects were being implemented. However, orders were issued
by the Ministry formally for constitution of State level Co-ordination
Committees (SLCC) comprising of State Government/agency officials,
representatives of the Ministry, HUDCO and NGOs to monitor the
progress of V AMBAY scheme in the States. In this regard, the
Committee are of the firm view that State Level Co-ordination
Committees should involve local representatives and also end
beneficiaries for monitoring the implementation of V AMBAY at the
State level to plug the loopholes or lacunae in implementation of
the Scheme at the grass-root level. The Committee also desire that
for further strengthening the monitoring of the Scheme at both the

information of the schemes so as to ensure that the benefits of
V AMBAY reach the genuine beneficiaries.
4. Integrated Low Cost Sanitation Scheme for liberation of Scavengers
(ILCS)
3.60 This Centrally Sponsored scheme has been under
implementation through Ministry or Urban Development since 1989-90
till 2003-2004. This scheme has been transferred to Ministry of urban
Employment and Poverty Alleviation w.e.f. 2004-2005 as regards
budgetary provision but its implementation has been effected by this
Ministry w.e.f. 2003-2004 itself. It provides for conversion of existing
dry latrines into low cost water seal pour flush latrines and construction
of new sanitary units where none exist to prevent open defecation.
The basic objective is to liberate the scavengers from the obnoxious
practice of carrying head loads of night soil and the scheme is being
implemented on a whole town basis.

numerous problems. The Committee express their doubt as to
whether manual scavenging could be eradicated by 2007 as envisaged
in the National Action Plan for Total Eradication of Manual
Scavengers given the present state of functioning of this scheme.
The Committee feel that it is a matter of shame for the country that
after 50 years of planned development, abolition of manual
scavenging is still a distant dream. Manual Scavenging need to be
eradicated at any cost. It is an insult to the humanity and in no way
can be tolerated. The Government should make earnest efforts and

5. National Scheme for Liberation and Rehabilitation of Scavengers
and their dependents (NSLRS)
3.71 The Scheme was launched in 1991-1992 with the objective of
providing financial assistance to scavengers handling night soil and
filth manually for their training and rehabilitation in the alternative
occupations. As a consequence of Hon’ble Prime Minister’s
announcement on Independence Day 2002 regarding total abolition of
Manual Scavenging by 2007, it was decided to ensure convergence of
different Schemes on the subject handled by different Ministries.
Accordingly the National Scheme of Liberation and Rehabilitation of
Scavengers and their dependents (NSLRS) was transferred form
Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment tot he Department of
Urban employment and Poverty Alleviation (Ministry of Urban
development and Poverty Alleviation) in the year 2003-2004.
3.72 Under the Scheme, assistance is provided for training in the
institutes run by the Government, local bodies and NGOs as per

32
TRYSEM norms. The training is given for a maximum duration of six
months. Stipend @Rs. 200 to Rs. 500 is provided depending upon the
training institute. Cost of raw materials, allowance for tool kit, etc. are
covered under the Scheme.
3.73 Apart from assistance for training, the scanvegers are assisted
for taking up alternate projects costing upto Rs. 50,000. This is funded
through 50% subsidy subject to a ceiling of Rs. 10,000, 15% of the
project cost as margin money loan which is shared between the central
and State Governments in the ratio of 49:51, and the rest is provided
as loan.
3.74 The entire subsidy is provided by Government of India as
100% grant. The margin money is provided by the State Schedule
Caste Development Corporation at a concessional rate of interest of
4%. Banks provide the loan component under their priority sector
lending. The National Safai Karamchari Finance and Development
Corporation(NSKFDC) is also now providing loans.
3.75 The Scheme is implemented by the respective State SCDCs.
In States where such Corporations have not been set up, the Scheme
is implemented by the State Governments.

7. National Slum Development Programme
3.93 The National Slum Development Programme (NSDP) was
initiated in August 1996. Under the programme, funds in the form of
Additional Central Assistance (ACA) are allocated by the Planning
Commission annually on the basis of slum population of the State/
UTs for development of Urban Slums. While the Ministry of Finance
releases funds to the States under this Programme, the Ministry of
Home Affairs also releases the funds to the Union Territories. The
States release the funds to the implementing Agencies as per their
requirements. The Ministry of Urban Employment and Poverty
Alleviation has been nominated as the Nodal Ministry to monitor the
progress of the programme in respect of States.
3.94 The objective of this programme is upgradation of urban slums
by providing physical amenities like water supply, storm water drains,
community bath, widening and paving of existing lanes, sewers,
community latrines, street lights etc. Besides, the funds under NSDP
can be used for provision of community infrastructure and social
amenities like pre-school education, non-formal education adult
education, maternity, child health and primary health care including
immunization etc. The programme also has a component of shelter
upgradation or construction of new houses.

39
3.95 Since the inception of the programme and upto 30.6.2004 a
total of Rs. 2,485.85 crore have been released by the Central
Government, and as reported by the States/UTs, about 3.74 crore slum
dwellers have been benefited from this programme.
3.96 Draft National Slum Policy is under the consideration of the
Ministry. Draft National Slum Policy, inter alia,  envisages an inclusive
approach for slum dwellers and granting land tenure to them on
‘tenable sites’ either insitu or by relocation.
3.97 When asked whether the Government has the data with regard
to slum population in each of big cities the Ministry in a written reply
stated that the slum development being a State subject, State
Governments survey and take stock of slums in their respective States.
However, Town and Country Planning Organisation (TCPO) conducted
a study on slums in 1995-96 and brought out a report titled “A
Compendium on Indian Slums-1996”. According to this report, the
slum population of 23 big cities (metropolitan cities) for 2001 is
estimates at 254.811 lakh. Slum population which was 148.249 lakh in
1981 increased to 188.659 lakh during 1990-1991 and further increased
to 254.811 in 2001. An attempt has also been made for the first time
during the census of India 2001 by the Registrar General of India to
collect detailed data about slum areas of the country particularly cities/
town having 50,000 population or more based on 1991 census. As per
the provisional figures of the census of India, 2001, the total slum
population of the 26 big cities (metropolitan cities) is 165.65 lakh.
3.98 The Committee note that as per study conducted by TCPO
slum population which was 148.249 lakh during 1981 increased to
188.659 lakh during 1990-1991 and further increased to 254.811 lakh
during 2001. The Committee further find that different data of slum
population have been indicated by two different studies conducted
by TCPO and census studies. As per TCPO the slum population
during 2001 in 26 big cities is 254.811 lakh but as per census of
India based on the Registrar Census of India, slum population in 26
big cities is 165.65 lakh. The Committee feel that sincere efforts
have not been made to know the slum population in the country.
The Committee recommend that the Ministry should first of all
conduct a study to know about the slum population in all the big
cities of the country in order to arrive at the correct estimate of
State/UTs. Besides there should be some mechanism to review the
data with regard to slum population after a fixed period of time say
five years. Such a data is required for formulating plan for tackling

40
the various issues like rehabilitation, relocation and providing
infrastructure and hygienic conditions in urban slums. Besides for
urban planning as well as finalisation of Urban Policy, such a data
is the necessary input.
3.99 The Committee are constrained to note the poor performance
of National Slum Development Programme. Upto 30 June 2004 a
total of Rs. 2,475.85 crore has been released by the Central
Government and about 3.74 crore slum dwelles have been benefited
from the programme which means that on an average about Rs. 662
per head was spent during the last eight years on slum dwellers
whereas according to the 2001 Census, there are 40.6 million persons
living in slums in 607 towns/cities in the entire country. The
Committee desire that the Government should enhance the release
of funds to the State under this Programme and should ensure that
release should be made for specific projects with adequate and proper
Central monitoring of the projects under the Programme.
3.100 The Committee further note that Draft National Slum Policy

8. Urban Reforms Incentive Fund Scheme (URIF)
3.101 The Urban Reforms Incentive Fund Scheme was approved
by the Government on 28.6.2003 with an outlay of Rs. 500 crore per
annum during the 10th Plan Period. The objective of the scheme is to
provide reform linked assistance to States so as to incentives and
accelerate the process of urban reforms identified by Government of
India, Ministry of Urban Employment & Poverty Alleviation. An
allocation of Rs. 500 crore is divided among the States/UTs on the
basis of their percentage of urban population to the total urban
population of the country. The incentive is given as Additional Central
Assistance (ACA) and is released as 100% grant by the Ministry of
Finance on the recommendation of this Ministry. For availing benefits
under the Scheme, States/UTs are required to enter into a prescribed
Memorandum of Agreement (MoA) with the central Government. 50%
of the eligible allocation during the year 2003-2004 was released as

41
incentive on signing of Memorandum of Agreement by the State
Government for the agreed reform areas and the balance 50% was to
be released on achievement of prescribed milestones, as indicated in
the Memorandum of Agreement. Releases for the year 2004-2005
onwards would depend upon the achievement of milestone for that
year as detailed in the Memorandum of Agreement. Initially seven
reform areas were identified. These are (i) Repeal of ULCRA;
(ii) Rationalization of stamp Duty; (iii) Reform of Rent Control Laws;
(iv) Introduction of computerised process of registration; (v) Reform of
Property Tax; (vi) Levy of reasonable user charges; and
(vii) Introduction of double entry system of accounting in Urban Local
Bodies. The guidelines under the scheme have been finalized and
circulated to the State Governments/UTs.
3.102 When asked whether the State/UT Governments were
consulted before implementing the URIF Scheme the Ministry in their
written reply have stated that the Urban Reforms Incentive Fund (URIF)
Scheme was brought to the notice of all the State Governments. Draft
Memorandum of Agreement (to be signed with them) was also
circulated to them. This issue was also deliberated in the Housing
Ministers’ Conference held on 12.9.2002.
3.103 When asked about the response from the State/UT
Governments to the Scheme the Ministry stated that most of the States
suggested that it may not be possible for them to sign Memorandum
of Agreements in respect of all the seven reform areas and carry out
all the reforms in one go, simultaneously. It was, therefore, decided by
the Government that weightage may be given to each reform area and
truncated Memorandum of Agreement may be allowed to be signed
so that releases may be made as per the weightage given to the agreed
reform areas and as per the achievement of the milestone(s) in each
reform area separately.
3.104 When asked about the details of States/UTs Government
which have signed Memorandum of Agreement (MoA) with the

Monitoring of the Scheme
3.105 The implementation of the scheme is monitored by the
Empowered Committee set up under the Chairpersonship of Secretary,
Ministry of Urban Employment & Poverty Alleviation, the Committee
assess whether a State has achieved a particular milestone in a reform
area before recommending to the Ministry of Finance for release of

Members of the Committee include Secretary, Department of
Expenditure or his nominee; Secretary, Planning Commission or his
nominee; Joint Secretary, Ministry of Urban Development and Joint
Secretary (Housing).
3.106 The Committee note that the objectives of the URIF is to
provide reform linked assistance to States so as to provide required
incentives and accelerate the process of urban reform identified by
the Government. An allocation of Rs. 500 crore is divided among
the States/UTs on the basis of their percentage of urban population
to the total urban population of the Country. The incentives are
given as Additional Central Assistance (ACA) and the outlay is
released as 100 per cent grant by the Ministry of Finance on the
recommendation of the Ministry of Urban Employment and Poverty
Alleviation. For availing benefits under the Scheme, States/UTs are
required to enter into a prescribed Memorandum of Agreement
(MoA) with the Central Government. Releases for the year 2004-2005
onwards would depend upon the achievement of milestone for that
year as detailed in Memorandum of Agreement. The Committee
further note that before implementing the URIF scheme, the same
was brought to the notice of all State Governments. Draft
Memorandum of Agreement (to be signed with them) was also
circulated to them. This issue was also deliberated in Housing
Ministers Conference held on 12.9.2002. The Committee also note
that most of the States suggested that it may not be possible for
them to sign Memorandum of Agreement in respect of all the seven
reform areas and carry out all the reforms in one go. Simultaneously,
it was therefore, decided by the Government that weightage may be
given to early reform areas and truncated Memorandum of Agreement
may be allowed to be signed so that releases may be made as per
the weightage given to the agreed reform areas and as per the
achievement of the milestone in each reform area separately. Till
31 March, 2004, 21 States and 3 UTs have signed Memorandum of
Agreements/Truncated Memorandum of Agreement with the Ministry.

43
3.107 The Committee are of the firm view that before launching
any scheme Government should first take the concurrence and
approval of the scheme from States and should also examine whether
adequate infrastructure exist with States/UTs to launch such scheme.
merely by indicating all the State Governments regarding launching
of scheme do not serve the purpose. Without proper follow-up
measure the targets can not be achieved. The Committee apprehend
that the poor progress in URIF Scheme is due to lack of coordination
and poor response of the State Governments. The Committee
recommend that the Government at this stage should adopt holistic
approach and the guidelines of the URIF Scheme be modified in
order to make it more viable so that the remaining States/UTs concede
to sign Memorandum of Agreements in respect of all reform areas
with the Ministry so that process of urban reform could be
accelerated. Schemes should not be launched superficially without
finding its relevance and whether the same can take off. In the
above case, this was not done. A perfunctory approach may lead to
waste of time, money, material and human resources. Such casual
move on the part of the Ministry is deprecated and they should be
careful in future before resorting to such puerile approach. The
Ministry should re-analyze the above scheme with feasibilities and
spell out the steps which could lead to its success.

CHAPTER IV
URBAN HOUSING
4.1 Housing and Human Settlement is a State subject. Each State
prepares its own action Plan. As per the National Housing and Habitat
Policy, 1998, the role of the Central Government is that of an enabler
and not of a provider. However, various schemes for housing and
human settlement implemented by the Government, provide additional
funds to the State Governments by way of grant/loan to boost their
efforts.
4.2 The National Agenda for Governance focusses on Housing for
all as a priority area, with particular emphasis on the needs of the
Economically Weaker Sections and Low Income Group category. This
programme envisages to facilitate construction of 2 million additional
units every year. Out of which 7 lakh would be taken up for
construction in Urban areas and 13 lakh houses would be taken up
for construction in rural areas. HUDCO is to meet the target of 4 lakh
units in urban areas and 6 lakh dwelling units in rural areas annually.
A target of 2 lakh dwelling units in Urban areas to be met by Housing
Finance Institutions (HFIs) recognized by National Housing Bank (NHB)
& Public sector Banks and the balance 1 lakh dwelling units in Urban
areas by the Cooperative Sector. Loans are disbursed by these agencies
for construction of dwelling units.

4.5 When asked about the salient features of recommendations
made by the National Commission on Urbanization with reference to
Urban Housing the Ministry stated that Recommendations of the
National Commission on Urbanization relating to housing are as
below:—
(i) Housing policy must aim a increasing the supply of serviced
land and low-cost shelter, improving and upgrading slums
and conserving the existing housing stock;
(ii) The State must facilitate housing and ensure access to basic
inputs. It should not become a real estate developer;
(iii) The sites and services programme should be extended to
cover the entire cross-section of society. Besides providing
housing, the programme should be used to generate
employment;
(iv) Apart from providing access to land, the housing programme
must also provide for finance, infrastructure development,
and community facilities;
(v) Inner city upgradation  and housing repair must be
encouraged;
(vi) Public agencies in the housing sector should be restructured
for fufilment of their new role as facilitators rather than
providers of housing; and

46
(vii) Rent acts should be modified to limit tenancy protection to
the poor and to the existing tenancies and to provide for
annual revision of rents to reflect increases in the cost of
living, the increases varying between residential and non-
residential premises and houses above and below 80 square
metres.
4.6 National Housing & Habitat Policy, 1998 has taken into account
these recommendations as is evident from the aims of the Policy which
inter-alia provides :—
Aims of National Housing & Habitat Policy
(i) Creation of surpluses in housing stock either or rental or
ownership basis.
(ii) Providing quality and cost effective housing and shelter
options to the citizens, especially the vulnerable group and
the poor.
(iii) Ensuring that housing, along with the supporting services,
is treated as a priority and at par with the infrastructure
sector.
(iv) Planning of urban transport is to be an integral part of the
urban Master Plan.
(v) Development of cities and villages in a manner which
provide for a healthy environment, increased use of
renewable energy sources and pollution free atmosphere
with a concern for solid waste disposal.
(vi) Using the housing sector to generate more employment and
achieve skill upgradation in housing and building activity,
which continue to depend on unskilled and low wage
employment to a large extent.
(vii) Ensuring that all dwelling units have easy accessibility to
basic sanitation facilities and water.
(viii) Removing legal, financial and administrative barriers for
facilities access to land, finance and technology.
(ix) Progressive shift from a subsidy based housing scheme to
cost sharing or cost recovery-cum-subsidy schemes for rural
housing.
(x) Progressive shift of rural housing strategies from target
orientation to a demand driven approach.
(xi) Using technology for modernizing the housing sector to
increase efficiency, productivity, energy efficiency and quality.
Technology would be particularly harnessed to meet the
housing needs of the poor.

47
(xii) Forging strong partnerships between private, public and
cooperative sectors to enhance the capacity of the
construction industry to participate in every sphere of
housing and habitat.
4.7 The Committee note that housing and human settlement is a
State subject. Each State prepares its own action plan. As per the
National Housing and Habitat Policy, 1998, the role of the Central
Government is that of an enabler and not of a provider. However,
various schemes for housing and human settlement implemented by
the Government, provide additional funds to the State Governments
by way of grant/loan to boost their efforts. The Committee further
note that the National Agenda for Governance focuses on ‘Housing
for all’ as a priority area with particular emphasis on the needs of
the Economically Weaker Sections and Low Income Group Category.
The working Group on Housing estimated shortage of 22.44 million
houses during the 10th Plan. 90 percent of housing shortage pertains
to the weaker sections. The Committee feel that keeping in view the
shortage of 22.44 million houses during the 10th Plan and 90 per
cent of shortage pertaining to the weaker sections there is an urgent
need to increase the supply of affordable houses to the Economically
Weaker Sections and Low Income Group category through a holistic
programme of allocation of land, extension of funding assistance
and provision of loan on low interest rate for construction of houses
for EWS category. The Committee also feel that to boost the housing
construction activities in the country, there is a need to encourage
and enlarge the participation of private sector, public sector,
cooperatives and individuals in this priority sector. The Committee
further feel that to overcome the enormous shortage of housing in
the country there is a need to encourage rental housing which
requires legislative changes in existing rent control laws. The
Government should think it over and come out with a proposal.

which earmarks substantial portion of its loaning pertions for weaker
